achira.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist bows too deep and asks, ever so formally, where the enormous bell hangs. Grandma Kane doesn't just point — she straightens up, sweeps her whole arm in a slow, ceremonial arc past the mossy steps and every lounging cat, all the way to the far tower, because when the distance is real and the company deserves manners, you don't jab a finger — you gesture, grandly, over there.
achira.reading_mnemonic: You already know あ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>あちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"ah-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, nothing hidden underneath.
achira.description: This is the polite, distance-marking form of "over there" — the one you use with strangers, customers, or anyone above you in status, not the clipped, casual version you'd use with close friends. Point far away formally, not with a jabbed finger.

akachan.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, by the vending machine, a hiker's toddler drops her snack and wails so hard her whole face floods the same deep, angry <kanji>red</kanji> as the ground splitting open on that hillside, glowing from the fire underneath. Nothing quiets a face that red. That furious red-faced bundle is a baby.
akachan.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly the pieces you already know: 赤 gives you the あか, and the childish ちゃん suffix tacks straight on after it, spelling out <reading>あかちゃん</reading>.

ame-v.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the window, watching the same drops slide down the glass, one after another inside their frame. Step outside now and those drops aren't caught behind glass anymore — they're landing straight on your shoulders. What's soaking you has exactly one name: <kanji>rain</kanji>.
ame-v.reading_mnemonic: This word keeps 雨's own taught reading exactly as taught, so it reads <reading>あめ</reading> — the same sound you already tied to the drops sliding down the window frame.

anata.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till breaks and starts beeping the same word at whoever steps up to pay — anata, anata — refusing to learn a single name. Customers give up introducing themselves and just answer to it, until the word stops being rude and becomes the only way anyone in that line ever gets addressed: you.
anata.reading_mnemonic: あなた is written exactly the way it sounds — plain kana, no kanji hiding a different reading — so the word you say is simply 「<reading>あなた</reading>」.
anata.description: In real conversation あなた is used sparingly — Japanese usually addresses people by name or title, and aiming あなた at a stranger or superior can sound distant or even confrontational; it is most naturally heard from a wife speaking to her husband.

ane.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, your older sister has already claimed the flattest washing stone before you're even awake, scrubbing yesterday's clothes while lecturing you for not helping. She never once asks if you mind. That unasked-for seniority, exercised at six in the morning by the water, is what (my) older sister names.
ane.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a horse comes down to drink beside her washing stone and lets out a flat <reading>ah, neigh</reading> right in her ear — which is exactly how <reading>あね</reading> sounds, and exactly why she never washes clothes there again.
ane.description: A plain, informal word for your own older sister when talking about her to someone else — not used to address her directly or to speak politely about someone else's older sister.

ani.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last good onigiri is one shelf away. Your older brother doesn't ask — he plants a hand on your shoulder, uses you as a step stool, and takes it while you're still off balance. That casual, lifelong right to shove you aside without apologizing is what (my) older brother names.
ani.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, he shoves past you and you catch the shelf edge with your knee. <reading>Ah, knee</reading>, you groan, doubled over by the onigiri — which is exactly how <reading>あに</reading> sounds, and exactly who just walked off without noticing.
ani.description: A plain, informal word for your own older brother when talking about him to someone else — never used to address him directly, and not the word used to speak politely about someone else's older brother (that is oniisan).

anna.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, Sei points at the vending machine improbably perched at the summit, far beyond arm's reach, and mutters that only that kind of machine — the distant one neither of them chose — would end up all the way up there.
anna.reading_mnemonic: This is another kana-only word, so <reading>あんな</reading> is simply read as written, with no separate derivation needed.

ano.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a goat sits down across the path and will not budge until you say what you are climbing toward. You point at the vending machine improbably parked at the summit, a speck against the sky, and groan ah, no, not that far. The goat only accepts things too distant to touch: that vending machine over there, that peak over there.
ano.reading_mnemonic: Nothing hidden in this one: it is written in kana exactly the way it is spoken, <reading>あの</reading>.
ano.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something far from both you and the listener, or at something you both already know about even when it is nowhere in sight. Stretched out on its own, with the first vowel held, it is also the ordinary hesitation noise, roughly English um, and carries no pointing sense at all.

are.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail you and a stranger both stop and squint at the vending machine glowing at the very summit, hopelessly far from either of you. All you can manage is a long flat ahh, and the stranger adds a defeated eh. Nobody is reaching it today. Not near you, not near them, just a speck up the slope — that over there.
are.reading_mnemonic: Kana only, said exactly as it is written: <reading>あれ</reading>, with nothing to decode.
are.description: Used for something far from both you and the person you are talking to, not merely far from you. It also does duty for a thing you both already know about but is not present — the that in that trip we took — which is why it turns up so often in conversation with no object in sight.

asa.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi bolts a plastic rooster above the konbini door that shrieks the instant the shutters roll up — never at lunch, never at night, only in that grey hour when the sky is still dim and the onigiri shelves are half-stocked. That first shriek of the day is morning, whether Koichi likes it or not.
asa.reading_mnemonic: Each dawn the rooster mounted above Koichi's door screeches <reading>あさ</reading> into his ear, and it comes out sounding exactly like <reading>ah, sir</reading> — a rude little wake-up call Koichi has never forgiven. That screech, not the sunrise, is what actually starts his morning.

asagohan.meaning_mnemonic: A rooster oversleeps at Grandma Kane's shrine and wakes to the sun already glaring off the enormous bell. He bolts down the mossy steps two at a time, scattering cats, because the priest sets out rice, grilled fish, and miso the instant dawn breaks — whoever reaches that tray first gets breakfast.
asagohan.reading_mnemonic: Every dawn a groggy monk stumbles toward the shrine gate mumbling <reading>ah, sir, go, Han</reading> at the boy stacking bowls, before Han even asks what he wants: <reading>あさごはん</reading>, already getting cold on the step.

asatte.meaning_mnemonic: The trailing runner is so far <kanji>behind</kanji> the pack he misses today's finish line entirely. He staggers past the sun's <kanji>day</kanji> window just as it flips shut — then flips shut again before he arrives. Two whole days close inside that window before he shows up, so nobody calls it tomorrow. It's the day after tomorrow.
asatte.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's vending machine, a hiker drops a salty tray of dried squid clean over the edge. It bounces ledge to ledge so long that two sunrises pass before it clatters to a stop below, and by then everyone agrees the <reading>a salty tray</reading> landed on <reading>あさって</reading> — the day after tomorrow.

ashi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, that mouth-topped pair of stopped legs is moving again, planted step after step all the way to the vending machine at the top, still barking orders down at itself with every stride. Whatever plants itself like that and carries you onward — that's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg.
ashi-v.reading_mnemonic: That same 足 already taught you two readings, and this word just takes the plain <reading>あし</reading> straight off it.

ashita.meaning_mnemonic: That same barred window from the <kanji>day</kanji> story shows up again, except the glass is still dark — the sun hasn't climbed into frame yet. You can feel it waiting just behind the horizon, ready to flood in the moment this window opens again. The day still queued up behind that glass is tomorrow.
ashita.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine stocks one item: a single <reading>ashtray</reading> that never fills, no matter how much ash hikers tap into it. It's saving that ash for a day that hasn't come yet — 「<reading>あした</reading>」, tomorrow, one climb away.

asoko.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a stray sock slips off the washing line and drifts downstream before anyone notices. By the time someone looks up, it's bobbing far off, snagged on a rock past the bend — not here, not nearby, just over there. That distant, can't-quite-reach spot is exactly what this word points at: over there.
asoko.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>あそこ</reading>, nothing more to decode.

atama.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, gym class lets out and everyone crowds through one narrow doorway at once - shoulders, bags, elbows, all jammed together. Except one part always squeezes through first, out ahead of everything else, cutting a path for the rest of the body to follow: the head.
atama.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeps one badly behaved llama tied up by the great bell, and it despises every visitor who gets too close, so it swings and clonks them square in the skull. The caretaker just sighs and warns newcomers the same way each time: mind <reading>a llama</reading>, or it'll crack your <reading>あたま</reading>.

ban.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic doors sigh shut for the day just as the fluorescent sign outside buzzes off, leaving one register light glowing over the empty onigiri shelf. That last dim bulb holding on while everything else goes dark is the whole picture: evening has arrived, and night is settling in right behind it.
ban.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker everyone calls <reading>Ban</reading> shows up right as the sky bruises purple, unlocking the gate for the evening service while the cats crowd the mossy steps behind him. His arrival marks the hour itself — <reading>ばん</reading>, evening settling over the shrine.

bangohan.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank at dusk, a tanuki has learned exactly when the cooking fire gets left untended, and it drags the whole simmering pot toward the water to wash its paws in what's left. The family gives up chasing it along the bank and just starts cooking a second pot, because dinner has to happen eventually, tanuki or not.
bangohan.reading_mnemonic: The father slams the door at dusk shouting <reading>bang, go, Han</reading> at the dog racing the tanuki to the pot, and by the time the door stops rattling everyone's already sitting down to <reading>ばんごはん</reading>, tanuki-free at last.

basu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, something huge screeches to a stop right outside the sliding doors, tires shrieking against the curb loud enough to rattle the onigiri shelf. The doors hiss open, exhaust rolls in over the till, and a wall of tired passengers shuffles out into the fluorescent light — this rattling monster is the bus, and it stops here every hour on the hour.
basu.reading_mnemonic: バス is written exactly as it sounds, so just read it as <reading>バス</reading> — the same sound as the English word <reading>bus</reading>.

beddo.meaning_mnemonic: A monk lugs a stack of futons up the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, planning to store them by the enormous bell overnight. Before he finishes stacking, half the resident cats have already curled into the pile and refuse to move. He gives up, tucks a blanket round the edges, and leaves them the shrine's new bed.
beddo.reading_mnemonic: This word is a straight loanword from the English word for bed, written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>ベッド</reading>.

bentou.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the improbable summit vending machine, a hiker unzips her pack instead of buying anything. Inside sits a perfectly packed rectangular box — rice, a pickled plum, a segment of grilled fish — eaten cold on a rock at the top. That neat travel box is a boxed lunch.
bentou.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, Ben trips over a root and sends his lunch tumbling downhill. He chases it hollering '<reading>Ben, my toe!</reading>' — say it fast and you land on <reading>べんとう</reading>, the boxed lunch he's sprinting to save before the crows find it.

biiru.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail's summit reward is one vending machine, impossibly humming after two hours of switchbacks. You feed it coins with shaking hands, and instead of water it drops a cold gold can that hisses and foams straight over your boots: beer, at the top of the mountain, before you've even sat down.
biiru.reading_mnemonic: ビール is written just as it's read, kana straight through — <reading>ビール</reading> — nothing to sound out beyond what's already on the can.

boku.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a boy waist-deep in the current catches nothing all afternoon, and when a fish finally leaps straight into his rival's net instead of his own, he plants his rod in the mud and announces to the whole bank that he, personally, will be the one telling this story later — not his friend, not the fish, him. That flat, proud claim to being the one talking is the meaning you want: I, said the rough, boyish way a kid says it.
boku.reading_mnemonic: He slaps his soggy fishing log down on a rock and reads the cover aloud in a gruff voice, <reading>book</reading>, <reading>book</reading>, until it slurs into <reading>ぼく</reading> — the plain, boyish way to say I that he now uses for himself as often as for the log.
boku.description: Used mainly by men and boys, in casual to neutral speech; it reads as too soft or boyish for very formal contexts and is rarely used by adult women.

booru-pen.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini till, a customer clicks a slim plastic stick against the counter, and a tiny steel ball rolls out of the tip, dragging a thin trail of blue ink across the receipt paper. Koichi doesn't blink — that rolling ball is just how a ballpoint pen writes.
booru-pen.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ボールペン</reading> is pure loanword kana, written exactly as it's read, straight from the English "ball pen," so there's nothing to decode.

boushi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji> from before, arms flung out, except Grandma Kane keeps wrapping cloth around its head for warmth, spiral after spiral, until the arms vanish under the layers and only a round knit dome pokes out the top — a hat, sitting where a baby used to be.
boushi.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat hides under the knit dome sitting on the steps. A visitor bends to pet it and the cat explodes out, making her yelp <reading>boo-shi</reading> — the same sound as <reading>ぼうし</reading> — before she realizes the dome rolling away is only a hat.

byou.meaning_mnemonic: You are buying an onigiri at the fluorescent-bright convenience store. The cashier hits a button on the beeping till and announces you have exactly one second to hand over your cash. You panic and throw your wallet at the counter, terrified of how fast a single second passes.
byou.reading_mnemonic: The wallet sails through the air, but a person standing right <reading>by you</reading> (<reading>びょう</reading>) snatches it. They pocket your money and walk out the door, leaving you to spend your last second in total disbelief.

byouin.meaning_mnemonic: A rowboat flips at the riverbank, and instead of a rescue crew, a whole hospital floats out to meet it — beds lashed to buoys, an IV drip swinging from a fishing rod, a nurse checking pulses waist-deep in the current. The patient is hauled onto the nearest buoy, wrapped in a blanket, declared stable before the clipboard stops dripping.
byouin.reading_mnemonic: The floating buoy at the riverbank turns out to be a tiny inn — a nurse leans out of the porthole and calls it the <reading>buoy inn</reading> for short. 「<reading>びょういん</reading>」, she says, tapping the sign nailed to the mast, and the soaked patient checks in like it's a hotel with worse pillows.

chichi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you're bragging to the clerk about how your father rewired the flickering sign himself. But every time the word for father leaves your mouth it comes out clipped and small, a fast double note like a chick cheeping under the counter, because that's the plain, low-key way you refer to your own father, never anyone else's.
chichi.reading_mnemonic: A chick has gotten loose behind Koichi's register and won't stop cheeping two identical notes at the customers. The sound lands exactly like <reading>ちち</reading>, the same clipped double <reading>chee-chee</reading> twice in a row, and it's the one word stuck to that particular chirp from now on.
chichi.description: 父 (chichi) is the plain, humble word for your own father, used only when talking about him to people outside the family — never for someone else's father, and not usually what you'd call him to his face. お父さん (otousan) is the polite counterpart: what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father.

daidokoro.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one door marked staff-only, and behind it he's wedged in a battered stove, a cutting board on two beer crates, a rice cooker plugged into the drinks fridge. Customers assume it's storage, but at three in the morning he's frying eggs back there between restocking onigiri — his whole kitchen, hidden in plain sight.
daidokoro.reading_mnemonic: Behind the konbini's staff-only door, Koichi knocks over green food colouring and hollers <reading>dye the dough, oh!</reading> as it splatters across the rice cooker — the exact sound of <reading>だいどころ</reading>, the cramped little kitchen where he cooks between shifts.

daigaku.meaning_mnemonic: The same wide-armed stretcher who's always bragging how <kanji>big</kanji> his catch was plants himself over the swaddled <kanji>study</kanji> child's roof of lesson notes and stretches even wider, insisting the canopy is huge too. He keeps stretching until the notes swell into a whole campus of towering lecture halls — the biggest school there is: a university.
daigaku.reading_mnemonic: You already know 大 as だい and 学 as がく — put them back to back, no softening needed, and you get exactly <reading>だいがく</reading>.

dare.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell rings itself in the dead of night. The cats scatter, the mossy steps creak, and no one is standing anywhere near the rope. Grandma Kane storms out onto the steps demanding an answer to the only question that matters: who.
dare.reading_mnemonic: Every night the bell rings and nobody's there, so Grandma Kane leans out over the mossy steps and bellows into the dark: who <reading>dares</reading> touch my bell? The cats scatter at the challenge in her voice, and that same dare is exactly the sound of <reading>だれ</reading> — the question of who it could possibly be.

denki.meaning_mnemonic: That storm-bred bolt punches through the rain and drives into a lightbulb on the ceiling, filament screaming white. Beside it, the curl of <kanji>spirit</kanji> that always rises off a hot bowl of rice streams upward too, feeding the glow. <kanji>Electricity</kanji> plus that rising energy floods the room: electricity, light.
denki.reading_mnemonic: 気 already lends you Kiki's giggly き, and 電 gives you でん — line them up and you get <reading>でんき</reading>, electricity.

denwa.meaning_mnemonic: The lightning that split the sky over your rain-streaked window doesn't fade at the glass — it dives down a wire and into a box on the desk. Out of the earpiece pours that same restless <kanji>talk</kanji>, tongue wagging nonstop, riding pure <kanji>electricity</kanji> into your ear. That's a telephone: talk carried on a bolt of electricity.
denwa.reading_mnemonic: 電 already gives you でん and 話 already gives you わ — stitch them together and you get <reading>でんわ</reading>, telephone.

depaato.meaning_mnemonic: A tower shop devours entire departments whole — one floor is nothing but shoes, the next is only teapots, and a man in a necktie gets trapped between six escalators that all disagree about which way is up. Every level swallows a different specialty until the whole building is just department after department stacked to the ceiling: a department store.
depaato.reading_mnemonic: デパート is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>department</reading> and you've already said <reading>デパート</reading>, no decoding needed.

doa.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini only has one way in: an automatic slab that slides aside the instant someone steps close, breathing out a soft whoosh right where the shop meets the street. New hires hear that whoosh and just call it what it sounds like, unchanged from English — a door.
doa.reading_mnemonic: This word is a loanword straight from English, written in kana exactly the way it sounds — read <reading>ドア</reading> just like the English word door that it borrows.

dochira.meaning_mnemonic: You've dragged yourself up the mountain trail to the one improbable vending machine at the top, expecting relief, and instead find the path splits into two identical forks beyond it. The machine hums, unhelpful as ever, while you stand there turning your head between both paths, asking the trail itself, out loud, which way.
dochira.reading_mnemonic: You already know ど, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>どちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"doh-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no surprises left to decode.

doko.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker's bag splits open and rice balls tumble everywhere. She scrambles after them, asking every passerby the same question over and over, all the way to the vending machine at the top: where did they go, where did that one land, where is the last one. The whole climb becomes one word, repeated: where.
doko.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>どこ</reading>, no hidden reading underneath.

donata.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hiker meets a stranger wrapped head to toe against the wind. Too winded to be casual, they bow deeply and ask with careful formality: might I ask, to whom do I have the honor of speaking? The mountain answers only with silence, and the polite question just hangs there: who, respectfully asked.
donata.reading_mnemonic: どなた is written exactly as it sounds, kana only — read straight through as <reading>どなた</reading>, no hidden reading to derive.
donata.description: This is the polite version of the plain word for who, used when asking after a stranger, a guest, or anyone you would address formally, the way English shifts from a blunt who's that to who, may I ask. Save the plain form for friends and family instead.

donna.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a clerk named Donna refuses to just ring anything up. She grabs every item — onigiri, drinks, gum — and interrogates the shopper: what kind of rice is inside, what kind of flavor, what kind of wrapper. The beeping till never moves on until she gets an answer to her only question: what kind of.
donna.reading_mnemonic: どんな is written exactly as it sounds — kana only, nothing to dig for — just read <reading>どんな</reading> straight through as it's written.

dono.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the onigiri shelf holds forty identical rice balls, and the man ahead of you has frozen solid, finger hovering back and forth while the till beeps behind him. Which one, which one, which one — he can never land on an answer, and now the whole line is stuck asking the same thing he is: which.
dono.reading_mnemonic: どの is written in kana exactly as it's read, with no kanji to decode — just sound out <reading>どの</reading> as it appears on the page.

dore.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school hallway has twelve identical doors, and behind exactly one of them a ball is bouncing. You work down the row knocking on every door, and each knock comes back the same hollow thud, so you start rattling handles instead. Twelve doors, one ball, and only one question left in your head — which one.
dore.reading_mnemonic: Written in kana just as it sounds, <reading>どれ</reading>, so there is nothing to work out.
dore.description: Asks you to pick from three or more things in view. When the choice is between exactly two, Japanese uses a different question word instead. Like its near and far partners, it stands alone as a pronoun and is not placed directly before a noun.

dou.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one impossible vending machine hums between the trees, accepting a coin no one on the trail carries. A hiker who just spent an hour climbing pokes button after button, turns to a stranger nearby, and asks the only sensible question left: how does this thing even work.
dou.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どう</reading>.

doubutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school announces a surprise visit from the local shelter, and by lunchtime every hallway smells like fur and nervous energy. Rabbits loose in the gym, a goat wandering near the vending machines, someone's parakeet shrieking over the PA by accident. Whatever has fur, feathers, or four legs and absolutely does not belong indoors — that's animal today.
doubutsu.reading_mnemonic: A teacher at Sei's school trips over the stray goat's hoof in the hallway and yelps <reading>though, boots</reading> as she catches herself against the wall. The goat stays entirely unbothered. Everyone agrees that yelp is the closest an English mouth gets to <reading>どうぶつ</reading>, and after today nobody forgets it.

doushite.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and charges double for the same onigiri, for the third night running. Koichi stares at the receipt under the fluorescent lights, not with a customer's cool complaint but a genuine, immediate splutter — why, how come, what is going on here.
doushite.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どうして</reading>.
doushite.description: どうして carries more feeling than a neutral question — it often doubles as an exclamation of surprise or frustration, how did this even happen, rather than a calm request for a reason, and it's the version heard far more in casual conversation than in writing.

doyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: On the calendar, Saturday's square holds a wooden cross planted into the page, dirt piling around its base — <kanji>earth</kanji> dug into the paper. Beside it crowds a tangle of feathers marking the square as a <kanji>weekday</kanji>, while a windowed frame shows the sun climbing to start the <kanji>day</kanji>: earth, weekday, and day stacked on one square make Saturday.
doyoubi.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the pieces you already know lined up in order: 土（ど）＋曜（よう）＋日（び）＝<reading>どようび</reading>.

eigakan.meaning_mnemonic: Every night, folding chairs fill Koichi's konbini parking lot — instant ramen cups, someone's dog draped over a cooler. A bedsheet gets clipped to the delivery truck for a screen, the shutter light doubles as a projector, and the whole block settles in to watch: a cinema built out of nothing but a parking lot and a bedsheet.
eigakan.reading_mnemonic: A giant film can rolls out of Koichi's walk-in freezer, crashes through the automatic doors, and unspools across the lot before anyone can grab it. He throws up his hands and grumbles that <reading>a giant can</reading> just opened a <reading>えいがかん</reading> right in his parking lot.

eki.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning another <kanji>station</kanji> platform fills with hoofprints instead of footprints — the local horses treat the place like open pasture. Today one gallops so hard it clears the ticket gates and skids onto a departing train, mane flying. Staff gave up chasing them years ago.
eki.reading_mnemonic: 駅's own taught reading carries straight over unchanged, so <reading>えき</reading> is exactly what you already know it to be.

ekiin.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning the galloping <kanji>station</kanji> horse thunders onto the platform, and it isn't the conductor who deals with it — it's the whistle-blowing worker in uniform who chases it back off the tracks before the first train arrives. Radio crackling, cap crooked, unbothered by any of this: that worn-out but unshaken figure is your station staff.
ekiin.reading_mnemonic: Over the radio the worker's reply crackles back garbled, just an <reading>echo in</reading> the tunnel — but that crackly <reading>えきいん</reading> is on every platform of this line, herding lost passengers back before the doors slide shut.

enpitsu.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, a boy chews the eraser end of a thin gray stick down to nothing, tapping the point against his desk until it snaps clean in half during the exam — the exact anxious shape and worry of a pencil.
enpitsu.reading_mnemonic: Sei checks the biology closet and finds the terrarium empty — the class hamster is loose again. She sighs, empty zoo, scrawling the note with the stub left in her pencil case. <reading>えんぴつ</reading> is that sigh: <reading>empty-zoo</reading>, written before the pencil's own lead breaks.

fuku.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine cats go bare all year, until the coldest morning, when she drapes a tiny knitted sweater over every single one. They strut past the enormous bell stiff-legged, dressed head to tail, mossy steps turned runway. None of them asked for clothes, but none of them takes them off either.
fuku.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a shivering customer grabs an armful of shirts off the rack and mutters <reading>"few, coo"</reading> through chattering teeth, too cold to finish a real sentence. The till beeps it through anyway, and the receipt just prints <reading>ふく</reading>.

fun.meaning_mnemonic: You are sitting on the riverbank with a massive pie. You use a heavy knife to chop off a <kanji>minute</kanji> wedge to throw to the ducks. The ducks completely ignore the pastry and aggressively bite your ankles for an entire minute.
fun.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is exactly what you learned for the kanji: <reading>ふん</reading>.

futatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The second raccoon inspects the snapped chopsticks on the table, short stick over long stick, and realizes they aren't cutlery anymore — just identical wooden splinters. It pockets both, satisfied that whatever it's counting tonight, the tally stops right there at <kanji>two</kanji> things, no broth-soaked evidence left to explain.
futatsu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 二（ふた）plus the counter つ, giving you <reading>ふたつ</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
futatsu.description: Like its sibling word for one item, this is a native Japanese number used for counting generic objects on its own, without a separate counter word attached — distinct from the Chinese-derived counting series paired with counters for people, flat objects, and so on.

futsuka.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon's broth has already gone cold once, but true to form, a second raccoon slips in and snaps its own chopstick to match the <kanji>two</kanji> lines exactly — and it only ever happens after the sun has climbed back through the window to open a fresh <kanji>day</kanji>. By the time the matching ritual is finished, that first day is gone and a second one has quietly started: two days, four paws, still nobody eating.
futsuka.reading_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini clerk trips over the same forgotten mop bucket two mornings running and lands flat on his back, socks soaked both times, groaning that his feet have gone <reading>footsore</reading>. Everyone at the register agrees this is just how <reading>ふつか</reading> goes — the second day is always the one that actually gets you.

gaikokujin.meaning_mnemonic: Follow the <kanji>person</kanji> already mid-stride past the slanted gate, headed <kanji>outside</kanji> — but this time they don't stop at the fence. They keep walking until the walls that wrap an entire <kanji>country</kanji> shrink into a smudge on the mountain trail behind them. Striding clean outside your own country's walls is what makes you a foreigner.
gaikokujin.reading_mnemonic: Each kanji keeps its taught reading in a row — 外（がい）＋国（こく）＋人（じん） — giving you <reading>がいこくじん</reading> straight down the line.

gakkou-v.meaning_mnemonic: The swaddled <kanji>study</kanji> child, still parked under its canopy of scribbled lesson notes, gets carried to the courtyard and set at the foot of the one great <kanji>school</kanji> tree. Roots tangle around the roof of notes, a bell rings somewhere in the branches, and the courtyard fills with kids at recess — canopy and tree have grown into one building: a school.
gakkou-v.reading_mnemonic: You already know 学 as がく and 校 as こう — chain them together (がく softens to がっ before こう) and you get exactly <reading>がっこう</reading>.

gakusei.meaning_mnemonic: The child camped beneath that roof of scribbled notes refuses to go home, and overnight the desk starts to feel like part of them — that's daily <kanji>study</kanji>. But they're not finished growing: the same soil that turns a seed into <kanji>life</kanji> is still working underneath them, a person still half-sprouted, still becoming. That's a student.
gakusei.reading_mnemonic: 学 gives がく and 生 supplies the same せい you already know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student, combining exactly into 「<reading>がくせい</reading>」.

getsuyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The squawking birds on your <kanji>weekday</kanji> calendar square are completely asleep under a thin crescent <kanji>moon</kanji>. They stubbornly refuse to wake up and look at the window showing the morning <kanji>sun</kanji>, because everyone is too exhausted on Monday.
getsuyoubi.reading_mnemonic: Since you learned the readings for these kanji already, combining them gives you <reading>げつようび</reading>.

ginkou.meaning_mnemonic: The figure who's always mid-stride, legs split wide, leaning into the step, never leaves the building — he paces the lobby, stamping passbooks between strides because he won't stand still long enough to finish one. Customers behind him catch the same itch to <kanji>go</kanji> before their money finishes counting — a building built around cash that never sits still.
ginkou.reading_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the onigiri shelf at 3 a.m. when a man demands gin. Koichi doesn't sell gin — he runs a konbini — but the man insists so loudly Koichi starts a private ledger, tracking yen owed for gin he never carries. <reading>Gin, Koichi</reading> mutters, ringing up onigiri instead, and the shelf becomes the block's unofficial 「<reading>ぎんこう</reading>」.

go-shujin.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> who strides in the door each night doesn't get his coat off before he's handed a list — go find the shoes, go find the remote, go find out why dinner's late. Everyone in the house treats him like hired help with a wedding ring: that's the respectful title for someone's husband.
go-shujin.reading_mnemonic: Jin the friendly giant barely ducks through the doorway before his wife barks: <reading>go, shoe, Jin</reading> — fetch her shoes off the shrine steps. That errand-running giant is exactly what <reading>ごしゅじん</reading> means: someone's husband, always sent to go find things.
go-shujin.description: This is the respectful term for someone else's husband, used when talking to or about the listener's family — not the word you'd use for your own husband. It leans on 主人 (master), so some speakers now avoid it for the gendered assumption baked in.

go-v.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, that same hooked hand reaches out from beside the vending machine, snagging snacks lined along the ledge. It's already got four stacked in your arms when the crooked hook swipes once more and lands a fifth off the top shelf. One hook, five snacks: that's the word for <kanji>five</kanji>.
go-v.reading_mnemonic: That practiced swipe already speaks the <reading>ご</reading> reading you learned for 五 — the clipped <reading>go</reading> you mutter to yourself right before you reach.

gogo.meaning_mnemonic: The instant the sundial's shadow vanishes into the <kanji>noon</kanji> line, the trailing runner finally lurches into motion — he's always <kanji>after</kanji> everyone else, and now he's after noon itself. Every stride he drags out from there on, still trailing that line behind him, happens in the afternoon.
gogo.reading_mnemonic: 午 already reads ご and 後 already reads ご, so 午後 just stacks those two sounds straight into <reading>ごご</reading>.

gohan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps end at a single offering bowl the cats can never quite reach: a small mound of plain white rice, steaming, set out fresh every morning. It isn't a snack and it isn't a whole feast — it's simply what's due at mealtime, the actual cooked rice sitting there and the meal built around it, both at once.
gohan.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a scrawny cat named Han races the shrine cats up the mossy steps for that rice bowl, and Grandma Kane leans out and yells <reading>Go, Han</reading> to cheer him on. By the time he wins, it isn't just rice anymore — it's <reading>ごはん</reading>, breakfast, served straight from the bowl he fought for.
gohan.description: This word literally names plain cooked rice, but in everyday speech it just as often means a full meal in general, not only the rice itself — asking someone if they've had gohan yet is asking whether they've eaten at all, breakfast, lunch, or dinner alike.

gozen.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the sundial's shadow first thing in the morning, still sprawled out long across the ground, well <kanji>before</kanji> it ever shrinks down to nothing at <kanji>noon</kanji>. That's the storefront's awning logic all over again — the part that greets you first, out ahead of the rest of the day. This whole early stretch, before noon ever swallows the shadow whole, is a.m., the morning half of the day.
gozen.reading_mnemonic: It's just the readings you already know, stacked together: 午 as ご plus 前 as ぜん gives you <reading>ごぜん</reading>, morning laid out in front of noon.

gyuunyuu.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, the morning delivery crate holds little paper cartons, so cold they sweat in the sun. A kid downs one in one gulp, gets a white mustache, and holds up the empty carton proudly to the whole team: milk.
gyuunyuu.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the lone vending machine hums. You press the button expecting hot tea and instead a freezing carton thunks out, and someone nearby gasps <reading>Ew, new!</reading> at the chill. That gasp is the reading: <reading>ぎゅうにゅう</reading>.

ha-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine dispenses exactly one item that day: a single chipped tooth, still faintly rattling, ejected after the last hiker crunched down on a stone hidden inside their rice ball. Everyone just runs a tongue along their own teeth, checking for the gap where a tooth used to be.
ha-tooth.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the nurse lets out one flat sound every time a kid limps in clutching their jaw — a startled <reading>ha</reading>, stretched thin like a gasp with nowhere to go. That same deadpan <reading>は</reading> is the whole word: the sound she makes over a broken tooth is the reading for tooth itself.

hachi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Those two strokes are still splitting wider at the bottom, the same spread that already meant <kanji>eight</kanji> when you met the kanji alone. Let that split happen four times over, fanned out beneath one twitching body, legs still moving until there are eight of them — a spider, standing on exactly the number this word names.
hachi-v.reading_mnemonic: This word borrows 八's own reading untouched, so it's read exactly <reading>はち</reading>, the same sound you already learned for the kanji itself.

haha.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, among the mossy steps and the cats sprawled everywhere, your mother doubles over laughing at some joke only she finds funny, the sound bouncing flat off the one enormous bell. That plain, unpolished laugh is exactly the humble word you use for your own mother, never for anyone else's.
haha.reading_mnemonic: Her laugh rings off the shrine bell as two dry, identical beats, <reading>ha-ha</reading>, the same flat sound as <reading>はは</reading>, over and over until the cats scatter. It's a plain, low sound on purpose, nothing decorative, matching the plain word it belongs to.
haha.description: 母 (haha) is the plain, humble word for your own mother, used when speaking about her to people outside the family — never for someone else's mother, and not typically what you call her to her face. It contrasts with お母さん (okaasan), the polite form used to address your own mother directly or refer to someone else's.

hako.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, you press the button for water. It grinds, hesitates, then drops a plain taped-shut carton instead, tumbling down the last few steps ahead of you. Nobody asked for this. The machine just started calling every carton a box, and now so does everyone who climbs the trail.
hako.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Koichi wades in to cool a crate of drinks and comes out numb to the elbow. He yelps <reading>"Ha, cold!"</reading> so sharply that the fishermen nearby start calling the crate itself by that yelp, and the name sticks as <reading>はこ</reading>.

han-time.meaning_mnemonic: You stare at the clock as the minute hand hits the bottom, turning the face into a giant exclamation point split right down the middle. That exact moment when the hour is chopped in <kanji>half</kanji> means it is half (past).
han-time.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading for this kanji, you know the reading for this word is <reading>はん</reading>.
han-time.description: You will see this attached directly to hour counters to say half past the hour.

hana-nose.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron plants itself ankle-deep and points its long beak straight up, sniffing the air to check whether the water's too cold to cross before wading in. That beak does the one job it's built for — smelling out trouble first — which is exactly what a nose is for.
hana-nose.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a new transfer student named Hannah presses her face to the cafeteria window, sniffing out the menu before anyone announces it. The other kids nickname her <reading>はな</reading> on the spot — that <reading>Hannah</reading>-nose never misses a smell, even through glass.

hana-v.meaning_mnemonic: Under the fluorescent glare of Koichi's konbini, someone has wedged a single potted plant by the onigiri shelf: one stem leaning hard to the side, its bloom spilling clean over the pot's rim. Customers keep stopping mid-reach for rice balls just to stare at it. Stem below, blossom bursting above — a <kanji>flower</kanji> where nobody expected one.
hana-v.reading_mnemonic: 花 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>はな</reading>, the same <reading>hah-nah</reading> sound.

hashi-bridge.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a delivery cart stalls at the water's edge, wheels churning mud. Someone drags two empty vending-machine crates out, sets them end to end across the current, and rolls the cart straight over the water without a splash. The crate-line stays there after — a bridge, built out of pure stubbornness.
hashi-bridge.reading_mnemonic: A cook at the riverbank burns a batch of <reading>hash</reading> browns and, furious, flings them one by one across the current. They land in a perfect line, crisp edge to crisp edge, and someone simply walks across on the hash line — which is exactly how you say <reading>はし</reading>.

hatsuka.meaning_mnemonic: The two raccoons are still hunched over their cold noodle broth, each guarding its snapped chopstick — the same two you met before. Every <kanji>day</kanji> new sun through the window finds them arranging the four chopstick halves into one perfect cross, the shape of <kanji>ten</kanji>, then doubling that cross because there are <kanji>two</kanji> raccoons at the table. After twenty of these sunrises nobody has eaten a single noodle: the twentieth day.
hatsuka.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs coffee straight off the warmer and spills it across the hood of his parked <reading>hot car</reading> right by the beeping till. Twenty days running he does this at checkout, and the staff now just call it <reading>はつか</reading> — the 20th, twenty days of the same scalded hood.

heya.meaning_mnemonic: Past the mountain trail's improbable vending machine, someone has wedged a plain door straight into the rock face. Push it open and there's nothing dramatic inside — just four walls, one chair, and quiet, built for the sole purpose of finally sitting down after the climb: a room, carved out of nowhere in particular.
heya.reading_mnemonic: The hiker collapses through that door, drops her pack, and sighs <reading>hay, yeah</reading> — worn out enough that even four bare walls feel like paradise. That sigh is exactly how you say <reading>へや</reading>, room, once you're finally inside one.

hi-sun-v.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the same window with a bar across it that you already know: the <kanji>sun</kanji> is climbing into the frame right now, filling the room with morning light. That one image was always doing double duty — window, bar, climbing sun — and standing alone it's already the whole word for sun and <kanji>day</kanji>, no second kanji needed to lean on.
hi-sun-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is written with the very kanji you already read as <reading>ひ</reading>, so the sound carries straight over — no new reading to learn.

hiru.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail the vending machine unlocks its second slot only once the sun sits directly overhead — no earlier, no later. Hikers who arrive starving learn to wait for that one narrow window, because whatever the machine drops then is the only lunch they get: noon, dead center of the day.
hiru.reading_mnemonic: A hiker collapses at the mountain-trail vending machine at midday, and it dispenses a bandage instead of a drink, printed with the words <reading>heal you</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>ひる</reading> sounds when the machine's speaker crackles it out at noon, every single day.

hirugohan.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the sports field empties for the lunch bell, and a stray dog times its raid perfectly, snatching a tray straight off the picnic table mid-sprint. Kids chase it in a lap around the track, but the dog is faster than any of them expect, gone with the whole lunch before anyone's fork is even out.
hirugohan.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher blows the whistle at noon and roars <reading>hero, go, Han</reading> at the fastest runner, sending him sprinting after the dog. He never catches it, but by the time he's back, someone's already laid out <reading>ひるごはん</reading> for the whole team anyway.

hito.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, someone rounds the corner: just two legs mid-stride, a body carried along above them, heading forward without dragging anything else behind. Strip away every job title, every role, every name — what's left striding down that hallway is simply a <kanji>person</kanji>.
hito.reading_mnemonic: 人 keeps the exact reading you already learned for this kanji: <reading>ひと</reading>.

hitotsu.meaning_mnemonic: Backstage after her talent show, the goat is handed a raffle box to count the night's takings. She digs through it hoping for more, but there is exactly <kanji>one</kanji> ticket rattling around inside, no stub, no runner-up prize. She holds it to the light anyway, satisfied that at least one thing tonight was worth keeping.
hitotsu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 一（ひと）plus the counter つ, giving you <reading>ひとつ</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
hitotsu.description: This is one of the native Japanese numbers used for counting generic objects, distinct from the Chinese-derived counting series paired with counter words for people, flat objects, and so on. It stands on its own without a separate counter attached, up through ten items.

hon.meaning_mnemonic: At the school, Sei kneels by the tree with that single flat line marking its <kanji>origin</kanji> and presses a stack of blank paper flat against the mark. When she peels the pages away, the origin's whole shape has bled through onto every sheet, and she staples the stack edge to edge — a bound stack of someone's origin, pressed flat and readable, is exactly what a book is.
hon.reading_mnemonic: 本 keeps the reading you already learned for it — read it as <reading>ほん</reading>.

hoshi.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi strings cheap fairy lights along the konbini ceiling, but half of them burn out by midnight, leaving a scatter of tiny bright points against black tile. Late customers buying onigiri look up and see a private sky punched with pinholes of light, one fixed point at a time. That single point of light, sitting alone in the dark, is exactly the word: star.
hoshi.reading_mnemonic: Two hikers reach the mountain trail's summit vending machine at last light. One collapses against it, and her friend blurts <reading>Whoa, she's</reading> done — then both look up to find a single point of light waiting over the ridge: the <reading>ほし</reading> that guided the whole climb.

hyaku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane lights one stick of incense at the shrine, and the smoke catches the white glow off the mossy steps until it multiplies before her eyes, exactly like that lone stroke stacking over the whiteness. By the time she looks up, the courtyard cats have multiplied to match — a whole <kanji>hundred</kanji> of them prowling the steps.
hyaku-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 百 by itself, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>ひゃく</reading>.

ichi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Judging her own talent show yet again, the smug goat holds up a single hoof and announces the score before anyone can ask: <kanji>one</kanji> out of one. There was only ever one entrant, one stage, one strip of dirt to stand on, so the number was settled before the show even began. She says it like a verdict, not a count: one.
ichi-v.reading_mnemonic: One line, one reading: 一 alone still reads <reading>いち</reading>, the same reading you already learned for it standing by itself.

ie.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hermit crab stops dragging its blistered shell. It wedges into a hollow rock at the trail's edge, lines up four pinecones in the doorway like doormats, and won't budge again. That hollow rock, doormats and all, is officially somebody's house — the crab has made itself a home.
ie.reading_mnemonic: A builder named Ei nails one crooked wall onto that same hollow rock and steps back beaming, waiting for someone to ask about the roof. Instead he throws both arms up and shouts <reading>いえ</reading>, which lands on the ear exactly like an English <reading>yay</reading>, and declares the one wall a finished house.

ikaga.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat dragging a rice offering off the shrine's mossy steps. Instead of shouting, she bows a fraction and asks, syrupy with formality, how the day has been treating it. The cat freezes mid-theft, offering still in its mouth, trapped by the world's politest how. Courtesy, not curiosity, is the whole word.
ikaga.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いかが</reading>」.

ikura.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself up the mountain trail to the vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting water. The display keeps climbing past every price he's paid for a drink, digit by digit, as he jabs the button asking how much this could possibly cost. It never stops long enough to answer — the only punchline the machine needs.
ikura.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくら</reading>」.
ikura.description: いくら written this way is also the everyday word for salmon roe, the bright orange fish eggs served over rice — a completely different word that happens to share the same sound and spelling. Context sorts them out fast: paired with a price or a question, it means how much; sitting on a plate, it means the food.

ikutsu.meaning_mnemonic: A kid parked at Koichi's till points at the leaning tower of onigiri and demands how many are stacked there. Koichi starts counting, and halfway through, the kid swivels and asks the identical question about his age. The tower wobbles, forgotten, as Koichi answers both with the same flat number — how many and how old are one demand wearing two coats to this kid.
ikutsu.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくつ</reading>」.

ima.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat ducks under the eaves the instant the rain starts — exactly the <kanji>now</kanji> image, a person taking cover under a wide roof, caring about nothing before or after. It won't budge from that dry spot even when the enormous bell rings, because for that cat there is no later, only this exact drip-free moment: now.
ima.reading_mnemonic: This word is just 今 read with the kun'yomi you already know, standing alone as 「<reading>いま</reading>」.

imouto.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the small girl who insists on carrying her own backpack up the mountain trail, refuses help, then sits down halfway and cries until someone caves and carries both the backpack and her. That stubborn, still-needs-looking-after littlest-girl energy is exactly a younger sister.
imouto.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the small girl stubs her toe on a root and yelps three sharp sounds — <reading>ee, moh, toe</reading> — before anyone can catch her. The hiker behind logs it plainly as <reading>いもうと</reading>, the toe-stubbing little sister, and keeps climbing.

inu.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening a dog parks himself outside Koichi's konbini, nose pressed to the glass, staring at the onigiri shelf like it personally wronged him. He never begs, never barks — just stands there radiating quiet judgment until someone caves and brings one out. That silent, immovable stare is what dog means here.
inu.reading_mnemonic: A new part-timer trips over the dog camped by Koichi's door and asks if he's some kind of mascot. Koichi shakes his head: he's just <reading>いぬ</reading>, plain and simple, and the easiest way to hold onto that is to hear it as <reading>in new</reading> — like he wandered in new and never left.

isha.meaning_mnemonic: A goldfish that stopped blinking gets carried into the clinic, though goldfish famously have no eyelids. The receptionist doesn't even look up — stranger visits happen weekly. When your name is finally called, the person in the white coat with a stethoscope swinging off one ear is exactly who you came for: the doctor.
isha.reading_mnemonic: The woman in the white coat introduces herself as <reading>Isha</reading>, which sounds more like she should be selling produce at a stall. But she's the sharpest <reading>いしゃ</reading> in the building, diagnosing your cough before you've finished coughing it.

isu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a heavy wooden seat with a tall carved back, and look closely — the carving is shaped exactly like a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide the way it always reaches. Those flung-out arms become the armrests, the swaddling becomes the seat, and the whole piece of furniture is built around that one reaching shape: a chair.
isu.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker spots the only bench and calls out to her friend, 'Ee, <reading>Sue</reading>, over here!' as she drops onto it with a groan. The two sounds run together into <reading>いす</reading> — the exact sigh of relief you make cornering the one thing at the summit built for sitting.

itsu.meaning_mnemonic: A heron standing in the shallows at the riverbank wears a wristwatch and answers questions for free. You ask about the water going down: it's two. You ask about the ferry: it's two. You ask about getting your own watch back off its leg: it's two. Ask a heron anything and it hands you a time, so the question you are really asking is when.
itsu.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, so <reading>いつ</reading> is both the spelling and the reading — nothing to decode.
itsu.description: English lets you say when for both the question and the joining word, as in the sentence about what happens when it rains. This word only does the question. The joining sense uses different grammar entirely.

itsuka.meaning_mnemonic: The hooked hand sweeps the shelf one more time, snagging snacks until the last crooked pull lands a perfect <kanji>five</kanji>, its fifth catch of the morning. By the time it stacks them by the window, the bar overhead has swung wide and the <kanji>sun</kanji> is climbing into a fresh <kanji>day</kanji> — five snacks, five days counted off on the shelf.
itsuka.reading_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, the hiker stops at the lone vending machine and <reading>eats a</reading> whole bag of chips — her fifth stop like this today. She sighs and calls it <reading>いつか</reading>, day five of pretending she'll pace herself.

itsutsu.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, your arm still cramped into the hooked shape from the character for <kanji>five</kanji> reaching sideways. Coins drop, cans thunk out one after another, and on the fifth thunk your hooked hand snags it before it hits the dirt. Five cans lined up at your feet, caught in one long, aching reach: five things.
itsutsu.reading_mnemonic: 五 already carries the reading <reading>いつ</reading>, and つ stays つ, giving you exactly <reading>いつつ</reading> — five things, straight from the readings you already know.

jibun-time.meaning_mnemonic: You drag a heavy pie all the way up the steep mountain trail to check the <kanji>time</kanji> closer to the sun. You chop it into a tiny <kanji>part</kanji> to act as a sundial needle on a flat rock. A hawk immediately swoops down and steals the slice, leaving you with absolutely no idea what time (of day) it is.
jibun-time.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the exact kanji readings you already know, making it <reading>じぶん</reading>.

jibun.meaning_mnemonic: Back at the pie you already sliced into eight equal <kanji>parts</kanji> to understand it, one wedge never gets claimed - it just sits alone on the plate while Grandma Kane's cats fight over the rest. That unclaimed slice belongs to nobody else; it's yours alone, the one <kanji>part</kanji> you can never hand off. That stubborn leftover wedge is oneself.
jibun.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a rower's <reading>jib</reading> - the small forward sail - swings loose and snags a stray <reading>bun</reading> right out of someone else's hands. He doesn't offer a single bite to anyone rowing beside him; that jib-and-bun grab, <reading>じぶん</reading>, is entirely his own business: oneself.

jikan.meaning_mnemonic: You are tracking the <kanji>time</kanji> by watching the sun climb the sky. But when it hits the <kanji>interval</kanji> of the open gate, the sun gets completely wedged in the gap. It stops moving, which means all the time / hours in the world have frozen.
jikan.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made of kanji you already learned, the reading is just <reading>じかん</reading>.

jisho.meaning_mnemonic: Long after the <kanji>write</kanji> sun has sunk below your notebook and your hand is still moving on its own from that daily ritual, the pile of scribbled pages has grown so thick it needs its own spine. You bind the whole towering stack into one fat volume you flip through every time you're stuck on a word — a book that exists only to make writing easier: a dictionary.
jisho.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the crow swoops down, snatches the book off your desk, and squawks '<reading>じしょ</reading>!' — which sounds exactly like someone yelling '<reading>gee, show!</reading>' as he flips through it hunting for a word he can't recognize, refusing to give it back until he finds it.

juu-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till beeps once for every raised finger, and the cashier keeps raising both hands until every finger is up, tracing the same <kanji>ten</kanji> cross in the air. The till stops beeping exactly when both hands are full — ten, and not one beep more.
juu-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 十 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>じゅう</reading>.

kaban.meaning_mnemonic: After the last bell at Sei's school, someone crams gym shoes, dog-eared workbooks, and a crumpled umbrella into one straining canvas sack, then wrestles the zipper shut over the bulge as it clears the sports field. That overstuffed sack slung over a shoulder is just a bag doing its job.
kaban.reading_mnemonic: <reading>かばん</reading> is plain kana, written exactly as it sounds, no kanji reading to derive here.

kado.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini sits right on the corner, and a delivery van cuts the turn too sharp. It clips the onigiri shelf through the window, spins once, and wedges itself nose-first into the exact corner of the building — where it stays, blocking the corner entrance for the rest of the shift.
kado.reading_mnemonic: The van's <reading>car door</reading> pops open on impact and won't shut again — it hangs there at the corner of the konbini like a broken wing. Koichi just tapes a sign to it: this is the corner now. That crumpled car door is exactly how you remember <reading>かど</reading>.

kagi.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail is, inexplicably, padlocked. A hiker pats down every pocket of their khaki trousers, harder and harder, until deep in the last one something small and metal turns up — the only thing standing between them and a can of tea: the key that finally opens the lock.
kagi.reading_mnemonic: The hiker digs through <reading>khaki</reading> pocket after khaki pocket, patting each one flat, until the last gives up a small metal shape with a jingle. That frantic pocket search is <reading>かぎ</reading> — the key that finally unlocks the padlock chaining the vending machine shut.
kagi.description: In Japanese, 鍵 covers both the physical key and the lock it opens — context decides which one is meant, where English normally reaches for two separate words.

kaisha.meaning_mnemonic: The landlord insists the view improves productivity, so the office gets hauled up the steep mountain trail — desks wedged between boulders, the printer jamming two switchbacks from the top. The boss holds the meeting by the vending machine, tapping his coffee like a whiteboard. A hiker asks if this is really a company. It is.
kaisha.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, <reading>Kai shares</reading> his last rice ball with a gasping hiker, then checks his watch — his 「<reading>かいしゃ</reading>」 starts at nine and he still has to jog back down. Kai shares his snacks the same way he shares deadlines: reluctantly, but right on schedule.

kaishain.meaning_mnemonic: Every floor the elevator stops at, the same tired figure in a grey suit steps on, straightens a badge, staples one form, and steps off two floors later to do it all again. Nobody remembers his name, only his badge and his sigh. That endless loop of suit, badge, and paperwork is exactly what the word means: company employee.
kaishain.reading_mnemonic: His badge, half-covered by his tie, reads <reading>Kai Shain</reading> in blocky letters — no one at the company can pronounce it right, but everyone recognizes that a <reading>かいしゃいん</reading> like him has been riding this elevator since it was installed.

kamera.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist raises a boxy black gadget with a glass eye at the enormous bell and shouts the thing's own name at it. The flash pops, every cat on the mossy steps freezes mid-leap, and the little screen lights up with the shot: a camera, catching cats that never agreed to sit still.
kamera.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, no kanji to decode — just say what you see: <reading>カメラ</reading>.

kami-hair.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the resident cats leaps onto a visitor's shoulders and burrows straight into the long dark strands hanging past her collar, kneading and refusing to leave. Grandma Kane just laughs, ringing the mossy steps clean, and says the cat has finally found the hair it always wanted to nest in.
kami-hair.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane calls that shrine cat <reading>Cami</reading>, and Cami spends every visit nesting in the same visitor's <reading>かみ</reading>, purring against her scalp. Grandma Kane rings the enormous bell to shoo her off, but Cami just digs deeper into the かみ and refuses to move.

kami-paper.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats leap along the mossy steps and swat every fortune slip off the branches, until by dusk the ground is drifted white with thin square sheets — not snow, just fallen paper, blanketing the whole shrine before Grandma Kane can ring the bell.
kami-paper.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat pawing through the drifted fortune slips and snaps, come, me! — meaning drop it and follow her to the shrine office. <reading>かみ</reading> is that snap: <reading>come-me</reading>, aimed at a cat sitting on a pile of shrine paper.

kanojo.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi points across the konbini at the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> restocking the onigiri shelf, arm sweeping the row into place. He doesn't explain, just tilts his head and grins: that's the one he's been talking about all week. You don't need more than that look to know she's his girlfriend, and now you know who she is too.
kanojo.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she keeps introducing the same woman standing by the bell alongside a man named Joe: Kane, and Joe. Say it fast — <reading>Kane-Joe</reading> — and you land on <reading>かのじょ</reading>, the word for her, the girlfriend everyone at the shrine already knows by name.

kao.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat named Botan leaps onto the offering bowl and stares down at the water pooled inside it, hunting the strange animal staring back. It takes three tail-lashes before Botan realizes the intruder blinks whenever she blinks — it is her own face, staring up out of the water.
kao.reading_mnemonic: A cow wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine and butts the shrine bell aside just to see what's cooking. The monk grabs the <reading>cow</reading> by the horns and yells right into its <reading>かお</reading> — but its blank face never changes.

karada.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, the gym teacher lines everyone up and makes them stretch every part at once — arms, legs, back, neck — until the whole trembling row moves as a single shuddering unit. She points down the line and names it plainly: the body, all of it, working together.
karada.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher barks that this drill works the whole <reading>car, duh</reading> — she means the whole <reading>からだ</reading>, obviously, and nobody laughs because she's still holding the whistle. からだ, she repeats, jabbing a finger at each kid's ribs to prove her point.

kare.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron keeps prying the side mirror off a toy car and dropping it at the feet of whichever man happens to be standing closest, like a tiny crown. The locals start calling that unlucky guy by the same word every single time — and since he's always some woman's boyfriend waiting there for her, the word settles on him: he, boyfriend.
kare.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron drops a plastic toy <reading>car</reading> at your feet, and someone mutters <reading>かれ</reading>, eh, nodding toward whichever man it landed nearest — and the name sticks to him alone, every single time the bird does it.

kasa.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the sky cracks open and dumps a whole second river down onto the first one. A fisherman yanks a bent bamboo frame out of his tackle box, stretches waxed paper across the ribs, and pops it open over his head just before he's soaked through — that bent, stretched frame is an umbrella.
kasa.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the rain arrives as one long <reading>cascade</reading> — clip off just the front half, said fast, and you get <reading>かさ</reading>, the umbrella the fisherman snaps open to survive it.

kawa-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, you crouch to rinse your hands and watch three currents braid together exactly the way you learned to see them: three flowing lines side by side. Cup your palms and the water doesn't care about the drawing — it just runs, cold and fast, over your fingers. That current has a name: <kanji>river</kanji>.
kawa-v.reading_mnemonic: 川 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>かわ</reading>, the same <reading>kah-wah</reading> sound.

kayoubi.meaning_mnemonic: You flip your calendar to check the <kanji>weekday</kanji>, but the square for today's <kanji>day</kanji> is completely charred. Looking closely, a tiny sparking figure made of <kanji>fire</kanji> is running around inside the window frame, burning up the paper. You sigh. The calendar always bursts into flames on Tuesday.
kayoubi.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading for each kanji, you can simply put them together to form <reading>かようび</reading>.

kaze-wind.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic door sticks open and a sudden gust roars in, sending the entire onigiri shelf toppling and every plastic bag in the store leaping off its hook at once. He just stands at the till, beeping through the chaos, muttering that it's too much wind for one small door.
kaze-wind.reading_mnemonic: Koichi swears the same draft <reading>causes</reading> the shelf to fall every single morning, and he's taken to yelling <reading>かぜ</reading> at the door like it's a curse word, until the whole konbini staff starts shouting it whenever a gust rolls through.

kazoku.meaning_mnemonic: Zookeeper Zoe stopped filing her animals by species years ago. Now every enclosure is sorted by family: otters piled in one tank, meerkats packed into one den, and the daily headcount sheet has only one column, because at her zoo the only unit that ever matters is the whole family showing up together.
kazoku.reading_mnemonic: Every evening Zoe cups her hands at the gate and calls out, a shout that lands in your ear as <reading>call-a-zoo, koo</reading>, the same two beats as <reading>かぞく</reading>. Every parent and cub trots out together the second they hear it, because that call means the whole family, not one animal.

keikan.meaning_mnemonic: Someone's been dumping fish traps along the riverbank at night, and every trap turns up empty by morning except the one time a figure in a sharp uniform wades in at dawn, hauls the traps out by hand, and confiscates the lot without a word. That quiet, uniformed figure standing ankle-deep in river mud is exactly what the word means: police officer.
keikan.reading_mnemonic: The uniformed figure flashes a badge and introduces herself only as <reading>Kay Kahn</reading> — and the raccoon mid-heist at the fish trap doesn't even try to run, because everyone on this riverbank knows a <reading>けいかん</reading> named Kay Kahn always gets her culprit.

keitai.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the new clerk Kei ties his phone to his belt with butcher's string before every shift, certain he won't survive the beeping till without it. By closing time the string has looped him to the register three times over, and everyone has stopped calling it a phone — it's just his mobile phone now.
keitai.reading_mnemonic: Picture the manager at Koichi's konbini shouting across the shop as the string tangles again: '<reading>Kay, tie</reading>!' — tie it down before it beeps once more. That shout is <reading>けいたい</reading>, the reading of mobile phone, the word Kei now answers to more than his own name.

ki-tree-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one trunk splits the mossy steps clean in half, roots shoving down into the stone and branches spreading wide over the enormous bell. Cats scatter into its shade every afternoon. There's no need to explain what's growing there — trunk, roots, branches, unmistakably a <kanji>tree</kanji>.
ki-tree-v.reading_mnemonic: 木 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>き</reading>, the same <reading>key</reading> sound, home to Kiki the tree spirit.

kimi.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the coach's whistle breaks, so instead of names he just barks the same word at whichever kid is nearest the ball — kimi, kimi — pointing, never naming. By the end of practice the whole team answers to it, the casual, jabbing word you'd only ever aim at a friend or someone younger than you.
kimi.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a scruffy stray dog answers only to the coach's shout of <reading>きみ</reading> — it sounds just like calling out <reading>key, me!</reading> while he jangles his whistle-keys — and the dog comes running to whichever kid the coach is jabbing a finger at.

kinou.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same barred window from the <kanji>day</kanji> story, sun and all — except now it's already downriver. The current has carried the whole sunlit frame past the bank, out past where you could ever wade in after it. Whatever daylight you missed while it drifted by is gone for good: yesterday.
kinou.reading_mnemonic: Every evening, Grandma Kane's shrine cats knock her <reading>keno</reading> ticket off the mossy steps, and by the time she finds it, the numbers already belong to a closed draw. She reads them anyway and sighs 「<reading>きのう</reading>」 — already over, every time.

kinyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: You go into Koichi's konbini to buy a single onigiri to start your <kanji>day</kanji>. When the till beeps, Koichi doesn't ask for regular yen; he demands a literal pile of <kanji>gold</kanji>. You complain that this is the only <kanji>weekday</kanji> he does this, and hand over your treasure because it is Friday.
kinyoubi.reading_mnemonic: This word is completely regular, so just read the kanji exactly as you learned them to get <reading>きんようび</reading>.

kissaten.meaning_mnemonic: Sei ducks out of gym class through a gap in the fence and ends up in an impossibly quiet shop three streets over — dim lighting, one old man refolding the same newspaper, a menu of drinks nobody at school has heard of. It is a coffee shop, and gym period never felt shorter.
kissaten.reading_mnemonic: Behind the coffee shop counter, the barista scores every espresso out of ten, and when one hits a perfect score, plants a theatrical <reading>kiss a ten</reading> on the cup before serving it. Regulars just call the place <reading>きっさてん</reading> and never ask about the ritual.
kissaten.description: きっさてん usually points at an old-style Japanese coffee shop — dim, quiet, often decades-old — rather than a modern chain cafe.

kitte.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, beside the one improbable vending machine, a <kanji>hand</kanji> peels a small sticky square from a roll and presses it flat onto the corner of an envelope before shoving the envelope into the summit mailbox — the little square that lets it travel: a postage stamp.
kitte.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker keeps licking the vending machine's sticky squares instead of buying tea, and the vendor barks <reading>quit it</reading> — she finally buys one properly, licks it once, and presses it onto her postcard: a <reading>きって</reading>.

kochira.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, on the sports field, the coach spots a shy transfer student hovering by the gate and waves the whole team over with one arm: this way, everyone — then, turning to the team, this is our new player. One gesture does both jobs, aiming a direction and introducing a person, which is exactly what this word covers: this way, this person.
kochira.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>こちら</reading>, nothing to derive.
kochira.description: This is the polite register: it is what you use to gesture someone toward a direction in front of others, or to introduce a person formally (a host presenting a guest, a clerk directing a customer), not casual chatter between friends about where something is.

kodomo-v.meaning_mnemonic: That swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms still flung wide from its own story, wriggles loose right in Koichi's konbini and topples half the onigiri shelf reaching for it. The till beeps in protest as a clerk calls out for whoever's kid this troublemaker belongs to — arms flailing, wrapping gone, still unmistakably a child.
kodomo-v.reading_mnemonic: Standing in the wreckage, the toddler points at the shelf and demands, <reading>Cocoa dough, mo!</reading> — garbled, insistent, again and again. That exact chant, <reading>こども</reading>, is what Koichi hears every time a small customer causes chaos in his konbini.

koe.meaning_mnemonic: A lone hiker stands at the edge of the mountain trail and lets out one enormous shout at the far canyon wall — not words, just raw sound thrown as hard as he can throw it. A beat later it comes back, fainter but unmistakably the same sound. That thrown, bounced-back sound, and nothing else, is what this word simply means: voice.
koe.reading_mnemonic: The hiker is named <reading>Coe, eh</reading> — that's literally how he introduces himself, flat and dragging the vowel out. So when he shouts into the canyon and the sound flies back at him a beat later, it comes back as <reading>こえ</reading>: his own voice, thrown at rock and handed right back to him unchanged.

koko.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane rings the shrine's one enormous bell every morning, but the rope has vanished among the mossy steps and circling cats. She stamps one paving stone and declares the rope must be tied down right there, jabbing the ground: here, here, here — and that exact stamped spot is where it's always been.
