koko.reading_mnemonic: ここ is pure kana, read exactly as it looks, so there's no hidden kanji to unpack — <reading>ここ</reading> is simply pronounced as written.

kokonoka.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> a fresh sun climbs through its window and lights one more switchback on the mountain trail, but you don't stop until the final bend, the one curled like a cane — the shape of <kanji>nine</kanji>. Eight sunrises come and go while you climb. On the ninth sunrise you finally round that hooked bend and lean your whole weight on the cane at last: nine days of switchbacks to reach the ninth.
kokonoka.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the hooked bend of nine, a vendor next to the lone vending machine sells nothing but <reading>coconut</reading>s, shouting the word at every exhausted hiker. It sounds close enough to <reading>ここのか</reading> that hikers now just call this spot the ninth — nine days of trail to reach a man and his coconuts.

kokonotsu.meaning_mnemonic: Hana reaches switchback <kanji>nine</kanji> on the mountain trail, exactly where hikers lean their hooked canes against the rock to catch their breath. Someone already got there first — not one cane but a whole row of them, hooked over the same ledge like abandoned question marks. She counts twice to be sure: nine things, propped together at the ninth bend.
kokonotsu.reading_mnemonic: This word simply takes 九's kun'yomi reading ここの and adds つ, the counter for physical things, giving 「<reading>ここのつ</reading>」.

kome-v.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, past the last switchback, hikers find the one vending machine standing improbably at the summit. Its slots hold no soda or tea — only small bags of hard, pale grains, unwashed and uncooked. A disappointed hiker buys one anyway, shakes it like a maraca, and trudges back down still hungry: uncooked rice.
kome-v.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the summit rattles her bag of grains and mutters '<reading>Comb</reading> through this later,' annoyed she packed the wrong snack. That mutter is exactly <reading>こめ</reading> — uncooked rice, the kind you rinse before cooking, not eat straight from the bag.

konbini.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's shop never closes, the till beeps without pause, and the onigiri shelf by the door restocks itself like clockwork at three in the morning. Someone pays a phone bill at the register while another customer photocopies a form, all before the entry chime finishes ringing. That does-everything, always-open little shop is a convenience store.
konbini.reading_mnemonic: コンビニ is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>conveni</reading>, short for convenience, and you've already said <reading>コンビニ</reading>.

kongetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The person under that wide roof stops watching the rain and looks up through a gap in the tiles at the crescent hanging there. They're not thinking about last week or next week — only <kanji>now</kanji>, only this exact sliver of <kanji>month</kanji> hanging overhead. Whatever's happening under that roof is happening this month.
kongetsu.reading_mnemonic: 今 already gives you こん and 月 already gives you げつ — stack them and you get exactly <reading>こんげつ</reading>, nothing new to learn.

konna.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi is standing behind his own register, holding up the onigiri that is already in his hand, insisting to the customer that no substitute will do — only this kind of rice ball, the exact one gripped between his fingers, right here and nowhere else.
konna.reading_mnemonic: This word is written the way it sounds, straight kana, so <reading>こんな</reading> is read exactly as it looks — no hidden reading to hunt for.

kono.meaning_mnemonic: You are in Koichi's konbini holding a waffle cone, and the beeping till will not stop until you name what you are buying. You do not know the word for cone, so you jab it at Koichi and repeat cone-oh, cone-oh until he gives up. He rings up whatever you are jabbing at: this cone, this onigiri, this rice ball — always the one right here in your hand.
kono.reading_mnemonic: There is nothing to decode here: the word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>この</reading>.
kono.description: Always attaches directly to a noun and never stands on its own. English happily says I want this with nothing after it; this word cannot do that, and a bare this needs a different standalone word. It marks the thing as near you, the speaker, rather than near the person you are talking to.

konshuu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> person, still huddled under their roof ignoring past and future, turns out to be standing right on the calendar page — the winding path of the <kanji>week</kanji> loops directly under their feet. Wherever they plant themselves is exactly where the loop currently sits. This week.
konshuu.reading_mnemonic: 今 already carries the こん reading and 週 already carries the しゅう reading, so stacked together in order they simply give you <reading>こんしゅう</reading> — no story needed.

koohii.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps furiously at three in the morning as a zombie-eyed customer clutches an empty paper cup, breathing out fumes so bitter the onigiri shelf seems to lean away from him. He doesn't order food. He doesn't speak. He just raises the cup, and the cashier refills it without a word: coffee.
koohii.reading_mnemonic: コーヒー is written exactly the way it sounds, straight through in kana — <reading>コーヒー</reading> — nothing here to decode, just read it aloud.

kooto.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine sells exactly one item: a stiff paper coat that unfolds like a cardboard crane. You climbed up in a t-shirt, so you feed it your last coins, unfold it, and stop shivering immediately. Up here, that stiff paper garment has one name and one job — it's your coat.
kooto.reading_mnemonic: コート is kana, so it is pronounced exactly as it looks — no kanji hiding a different sound. Read the four characters straight through and you get <reading>コート</reading>, the loanword transcription of English 'coat.'
kooto.description: コート is a loanword that also means "court," as in a tennis court — the two senses share one spelling and one sound, and only the surrounding sentence tells you whether someone is putting one on or standing on one.

kore.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you jab a finger at the onigiri closest to you, ignoring the whole shelf behind it. The cashier doesn't ask which one — pointing already decided it. That's the one you meant, this one, and nothing else on the shelf matters anymore.
kore.reading_mnemonic: これ is kana all the way through, no kanji hiding underneath — just read <reading>これ</reading> exactly the way it's written.

kotoshi.meaning_mnemonic: You invite the scarecrow to take cover under the roof right <kanji>now</kanji>. It's used to standing out in the weather for a full <kanji>year</kanji> at a time, but you decide it deserves to stay inside for this year.
kotoshi.reading_mnemonic: You find the scarecrow shivering in the snow, so you give her a thick winter <reading>coat. She</reading> puts it on with her stiff straw arms, grateful that <reading>ことし</reading> she won't freeze.

kouban.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lost tourist keeps ringing the enormous bell for directions. A patient officer steps out of a tiny booth by the mossy steps, cats streaming past his ankles, and points down the street to the actual police box — the booth that exists purely to rescue people from ringing the wrong bell.
kouban.reading_mnemonic: The officer's name badge just says Ban, and his sergeant radios him constantly: <reading>cope, Ban</reading>, another tourist's at the bell again. He sighs, straightens his booth's little roof, and steps out — that tired radio call is exactly how you say <reading>こうばん</reading>.
kouban.description: A 交番 is a small neighborhood police post, usually staffed by one or two officers, common on street corners and near stations — not the blue British police telephone box the English name might bring to mind. Locals stop by for directions about as often as for anything police-related.

kouen.meaning_mnemonic: A city block gets squeezed between an office tower and a train station, so someone covers it in grass, wedges in three benches and a rusty swing set, and leaves the gate open for pigeons and toddlers to fight over the last patch of shade. That leftover square of green boxed in by concrete is a park.
kouen.reading_mnemonic: A gatekeeper named <reading>Cohen</reading> stands at the entrance every morning and won't lift the chain until the sun clears the trees. Kids rattle the fence chanting his name until he finally waves them onto the grass — the moment he answers is the moment the <reading>こうえん</reading> opens for the day.

ku-num.meaning_mnemonic: That same hook is on closing duty tonight, yanking down the shutter at Koichi's konbini one slat at a time. It catches, drags, catches again — nine short tugs before the shutter seals shut, and the last tug is the one that lands on <kanji>nine</kanji>, alt reading and all, right as the beeping till goes quiet.
ku-num.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lone dove has nested in among the cats, and none of them touch it. When the bell rings, it doesn't screech — it lets out one flat <reading>coo</reading>, over and over, and that flat sound is exactly how this word is read: <reading>く</reading>.

kubi.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker finally reaches the summit vending machine and cranes forward so far to read the buttons that his head tips back on a long thin stalk, wobbling like it might snap clean off. Everyone behind him on the trail stares at that one stretched, straining neck.
kubi.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the trail, the hiker wedges his head into a stone <reading>cubby</reading> beside the vending machine to get a closer look, and now his <reading>くび</reading> is stuck fast in the gap. He twists his くび side to side, but the cubby holds on tight.

kuchi-v.meaning_mnemonic: That open square is still hanging there mid-yawn, exactly as you left it — nothing has been drawn inside it, because nothing needs to be. A hole with nothing inside was already the whole idea: it's just a <kanji>mouth</kanji>, caught wide open and refusing to close until you've said the word for it.
kuchi-v.reading_mnemonic: The kanji 口 already taught you both of its readings, and this word simply picks the plain <reading>くち</reading> one straight off it.

kudamono.meaning_mnemonic: After the last steep switchback of the mountain trail, a hiker collapses in front of the one vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting a cold drink — and finds every slot loaded with apples and oranges instead. Too worn out to complain, he buys one standing there. What that machine stocks at the summit is fruit.
kudamono.reading_mnemonic: Staring at the slots, the hiker <reading>could-a moaned</reading> about the missing drinks, but he's too exhausted to do more than mutter it under his breath, and that tired, flattened mutter comes out sounding just like <reading>くだもの</reading> — the fruit waiting at the top of the trail.

kumo.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine bell rings on its own one grey morning, and by the time she reaches the mossy steps, a thick grey mass has rolled in low overhead, swallowing the roofline whole and turning every cat on the steps into a silhouette. She squints up and just calls it the cloud sitting on her shrine.
kumo.reading_mnemonic: One of Grandma Kane's shrine cats, a fat grey tom the neighborhood calls Moe, sits on the mossy steps and coos up at the grey mass rolling over the bell. Regulars say he's only saying <reading>coo, Moe</reading>, but it comes out sounding exactly like <reading>くも</reading>, so that's what everyone calls the cloud too.

kutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the mountain trail, steep and endless, with that one vending machine impossibly balanced at the summit. A hiker collapses beside it, kicks off two mud-caked boots, and buys a can of tea instead of anything to eat. He drinks, sighs, and never puts the boots back on — leaves them right there under the machine as shoes for whoever runs out of nerve next.
kutsu.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail vending machine, a scruffy crow named Kutsu lands on the boots someone abandoned there and calls out sharply, <reading>coo-tsu, coo-tsu</reading> — the exact sound of <reading>くつ</reading>, over and over, guarding them like his own shoes now.

kuukou.meaning_mnemonic: A city block gets flattened overnight — grass paved over, buildings hauled off — replaced by flat runway under an empty stretch of sky. Nowhere to sit, nowhere to shop, just tarmac waiting for the next jet to lift into all that emptiness. That whole open, sky-swallowed lot is what people mean by airport.
kuukou.reading_mnemonic: A clockwork cuckoo escapes its clock and takes over the tower speakers, popping out every hour to screech instead of chime. Pilots stop listening for gate numbers and taxi in the moment they hear its <reading>cuckoo</reading> call — the whole runway complex ends up named for that shout: <reading>くうこう</reading>.

kyonen.meaning_mnemonic: You walk up to the scarecrow that has been silently watching the field for a whole <kanji>year</kanji>. Its straw arms are sagging and birds have built nests in its hat, clearly showing that it has been stuck out here since last year.
kyonen.reading_mnemonic: You are directing a play starring the scarecrow, but it keeps missing its <reading>cue. Nena</reading>, your stage manager, sighs and reminds you that it was much better at acting <reading>きょねん</reading>.

kyou.meaning_mnemonic: Ducking under that same wide roof, the <kanji>now</kanji> person refuses to think about yesterday or tomorrow — this instant is all there is. Beside them, through the barred window, the <kanji>day</kanji>'s sun blazes straight in, swallowing the doorway in light. That flood of light, happening right now, on this day: today.
kyou.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till only sounds its <reading>cue</reading> once every rotation, right as sunrise floods the doorway. Grandma Kane hears it, checks the light, and mutters 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — the one signal that tells her which day she's actually standing in.

kyoudai.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two toddlers wedged together at Koichi's konbini, each gripping the same onigiri and refusing to let go, both wailing that the other one started it. Neither wins, neither releases, and the clerk just watches the identical tantrum play out twice over — that matched, tangled squabble is what siblings means.
kyoudai.reading_mnemonic: The twins grab a pool cue and dunk it straight into spilled dye, striping the whole konbini floor like tie-dye. Koichi yells <reading>cue dye</reading> at the mess — and that yell is exactly how <reading>きょうだい</reading> sounds: siblings, always making double the trouble.

kyuu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The hook is still propped at the last switchback of the mountain trail, right where you left it leaning into <kanji>nine</kanji>. This time it's snagged a sock, blown off a line at the riverbank and dragged all the way up, caught fast on the hook at the top — bend nine, the last one, the whole climb done.
kyuu-v.reading_mnemonic: This word just keeps 九's own reading, so it's read exactly <reading>きゅう</reading>, the same sound you already learned for the kanji by itself.

machi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Hover over that same grid again — fields squared off on the left, the straight road cutting through on the right. Now watch it fill in: roofs go up along the road, a bakery claims the corner, kids race bikes past the fields. Roads plus fields plus everyone building a life between them — that's a <kanji>town</kanji>.
machi-v.reading_mnemonic: This word borrows the reading you already learned for 町 itself — <reading>まち</reading>, no new sound to add.

mado.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone at Grandma Kane's shrine so furious that a cat knocked over the offering bowl that they wrench open the wooden frame set into the wall and shout their outrage straight at the sky — mad, then oh, right as the frame swings wide. That opening they're yelling through, moss creeping up its sill, is a window.
mado.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches the cat sprawled across her offerings again and goes properly <reading>mad, oh!</reading> — the shout tears out of her as she yanks the wooden frame in the shrine wall wide open to chase it out. That startled yell is <reading>まど</reading>: the window she just threw open.

maiasa.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock that means <kanji>every</kanji> doesn't sit on a nightstand — it sits on the windowsill, cranked so tight that the instant morning light touches it, it detonates. Every morning: same crank, same detonation, same jolt out of bed. You can set your dawn by it.
maiasa.reading_mnemonic: Every morning, Sei's school gate creaks open for a boy called Asa — never late, never early, wound up like clockwork. Call the roll and mutter that <reading>my Asa</reading>'s here again, and you've said <reading>まいあさ</reading>. Same boy, same gate, every single morning.

maiban.meaning_mnemonic: That wind-up alarm clock that means <kanji>every</kanji> got smuggled onto the riverbank and buried in the mud with its key still poking out. At the same instant each night, the current winds it tight and it clangs itself off in the dark, startling every fish for a mile. Same hour, same racket, every night.
maiban.reading_mnemonic: Every night at Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell tolls once for a caretaker named Ban, who never misses a shift. The cats grumble that <reading>my Ban</reading>'s back on the mossy steps — and that's exactly <reading>まいばん</reading>: same bell, same watchman, every night.

mainen.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock gets planted in the field beside the scarecrow, refusing to ring until it's watched the same circuit: rice sown, grown, harvested, the field bare again. Only once the seasons finish that silent turn does the clock finally clank off — then winds itself back up to stand watch through it again, without fail. That's the clock marking <kanji>every</kanji> single <kanji>year</kanji>.
mainen.reading_mnemonic: 毎 keeps its taught まい and 年 keeps its taught ねん, combining exactly as expected into <reading>まいねん</reading>.

mainichi.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock that means <kanji>every</kanji> is bolted straight onto the window-with-a-bar that means <kanji>day</kanji>. It doesn't wait for the sun to climb — the second it rings, it drags the window open by force, hour after identical hour, and daylight has no choice but to show up. That's every day.
mainichi.reading_mnemonic: 毎 gives you まい and 日 gives you にち, so stack them exactly as taught and you get <reading>まいにち</reading> — no surprises here.

maishuu.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock drags itself onto the calendar page, walking the winding path one square at a time and ringing at every stop. Once it clanks around the whole seven-day loop and lands back at the start, it winds itself straight back up to walk the same route again, without fail. That's a clock stuck doing <kanji>every</kanji> single <kanji>week</kanji> on repeat.
maishuu.reading_mnemonic: 毎 keeps its taught まい and 週 keeps its taught しゅう, combining exactly as expected into <reading>まいしゅう</reading>.

maitsuki.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock sits on its shelf watching the crescent moon through the window, refusing to ring until it fattens, fades, then swings back to that same thin sliver. Only once that full swing is done does the clock finally clank off — then winds itself right back up to keep watching, without fail. That's the clock marking off <kanji>every</kanji> single <kanji>month</kanji>.
maitsuki.reading_mnemonic: 毎 keeps its taught まい and 月 keeps its taught つき, combining exactly as expected into <reading>まいつき</reading>.

man-v.meaning_mnemonic: Someone climbs a ladder to recount the banner's zeros herself, licking a finger to peel back each heavy fold of cloth. Her arms give out before the counting does, so she chalks a final total on the last scrap of space and declares the stall sold out at <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> onigiri — not one more, not one less.
man-v.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 万 read <reading>まん</reading>, exactly like the banner kanji you already know.
man-v.description: Japanese counts large numbers in blocks of ten thousand rather than thousands, so 万 anchors the whole system used for big figures. English commas group by thousands, so converting between the two takes practice — a million lands on a multiple of ten thousand here, not on a clean round number.

me-v.meaning_mnemonic: Above the register at Koichi's konbini hangs a security frame with two little dots for pupils, tilted so it looks like it's staring you down while you pick between the onigiri and the beeping till. That frame with pupils staring back is exactly the <kanji>eye</kanji> watching every customer who lingers too long.
me-v.reading_mnemonic: 目 already gives you this reading on its own — め is exactly how 目 reads by itself, so the <reading>め</reading> here is that very same reading, unchanged.

megane.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the librarian's eyesight gives out mid-shelving, so she bends two empty onigiri wrappers from Koichi's konbini into perfect circles, wires them together with a stray chopstick, and hooks the whole rig over her ears. The blur snaps into focus at once — she has just invented glasses.
megane.reading_mnemonic: A new student at Sei's school keeps insisting she isn't wearing glasses, but every teacher squints at her face and asks, <reading>Meg, uh, nay?</reading> — which is exactly how you say <reading>めがね</reading>, the glasses she is obviously wearing.

michi-v.meaning_mnemonic: You keep following that winding <kanji>road</kanji> up the mountain trail, switchback after switchback, until it stops being a hiking route — a delivery scooter buzzes past, a mailbox appears at the bend, gravel turns to pavement. It isn't a trail anymore; it's somebody's street. That's the word: <kanji>road</kanji>, the ordinary road or street right outside a door.
michi-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is read exactly like the kanji you already know: 道 is <reading>みち</reading>, so no new story is needed here.

mikka.meaning_mnemonic: Stack the <kanji>three</kanji> flat lines on top of each other and each one turns out to be its own tiny windowed frame with a sun climbing up through it — a triple-decker calendar. One <kanji>day</kanji> passes on the bottom line, then the middle one lights up, then the top, and the sun never bothers waiting around for a fourth: three days, no more, no less.
mikka.reading_mnemonic: Sei collapses after the third whistle blast on the sports field, and the nurse says she's gone <reading>meeker</reading> by the hour — flu, straight home for <reading>みっか</reading>, three full days in bed before anyone lets her back on the field.

mimi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, that dangling flap of skin catches the sudden beep of the vending machine echoing off the rock face before your eyes even register the machine is there. The flap swivels toward the sound like it has a mind of its own — proof that the whole point of an <kanji>ear</kanji> is hearing first, seeing second.
mimi-v.reading_mnemonic: 耳 already reads みみ on its own, so the <reading>みみ</reading> in this word is that same reading, said once for the character and now doubled for the word.

minna.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the tinny loudspeaker crackles once and a single voice booms through every aisle at the same instant, announcing a surprise scavenger hunt: onigiri, umbrellas, batteries, go. Every last customer looks up from what they're doing in the same second - not some of them, not most of them. Everyone.
minna.reading_mnemonic: みんな is written exactly the way it sounds, plain kana with nothing hiding underneath, so the word simply is its own reading: <reading>みんな</reading>.

mise.meaning_mnemonic: A hand-painted sign hangs above one sliding door: vegetable bins spill onto the pavement, a bell over the frame jingles nonstop, and the till keeps popping open from coins going in and out all day. Nothing about the place is fancy — just one small room built around handing things to people for money. That room is a shop.
mise.reading_mnemonic: A tiny shopkeeper mouse rings up every sale by squeaking the price twice, so customers just call the cramped counter <reading>mice, eh</reading> — say it fast enough and you get <reading>みせ</reading>, the shop everyone in town swears is run entirely by rodents.

mittsu.meaning_mnemonic: You're at the riverbank stacking flat stones into a cairn, the way the character for <kanji>three</kanji> stacks its own three flat lines. One stone, then a second balanced on top, and just as the tower wobbles you set down a third to steady it. Three stones, standing exactly as tall as the character taught you: three things, balanced and done.
mittsu.reading_mnemonic: 三 already carries the reading <reading>みっ</reading>, and つ stays つ, so together they give you exactly <reading>みっつ</reading> — three things, built straight from readings you already know.

mizu.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the riverbank where the streams splash outward in every direction, cold spray hitting your face. Cup your hands in that spray, and the streaks resolve into something you can actually drink: <kanji>water</kanji>.
mizu.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same sound you already know from 水: <reading>みず</reading>.

mokuyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: You arrive at Sei's school for a normal <kanji>weekday</kanji> of classes, but looking out the window, a massive <kanji>tree</kanji> has smashed right through the sports field to block out the <kanji>sun</kanji>. The principal announces over the intercom that classes are cancelled, which is typical for Thursday.
mokuyoubi.reading_mnemonic: You can sound this word out by stringing together the readings you learned for its component kanji to get <reading>もくようび</reading>.

muika.meaning_mnemonic: The eight stands tall until someone claps a lid on top, capping it down to <kanji>six</kanji>. That very lid turns out to be the window's bar swinging shut over the <kanji>sun</kanji>, sealing off one whole <kanji>day</kanji> at a time — six lids, six sunsets, and that's the 6th, six days gone.
muika.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a cow wades in to wash off and lets out six long moos in a row, counting each one on its hooves. On the sixth <reading>moo</reading> it wobbles and calls out <reading>むいか</reading> before toppling into the current — six days, six moos, one soaked cow.

musuko.meaning_mnemonic: That same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide, has somehow hauled itself up the whole mountain trail and is now feeding coins into the vending machine at the summit like it owns the place. A hiker asks the panting father trailing behind whose kid that is. He beams, chest out — that's his son.
musuko.reading_mnemonic: At the summit, the father spots a moose eyeing his boy's snack and bellows <reading>Moose, Coe!</reading> — the name of the trail's resident moose, shouted fast and clipped. That exact bark, <reading>むすこ</reading>, is what every hiker on this mountain learns to recognize as a warning about his son.

musume.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a girl in oversized cleats trips over the finish-line ribbon and drags the whole banner down with her. A woman in the stands leaps up, mortified and delighted at once, shouting across the entire field for her — this ribbon-tangled little disaster is her daughter.
musume.reading_mnemonic: Still tangled in ribbon, she turns to the snack table and asks sweetly, <reading>Mousse, may?</reading> — polite as anything in the middle of a disaster. That well-mannered request, <reading>むすめ</reading>, is the reading you're listening for.

muttsu.meaning_mnemonic: The lid clamps down on eight again, this time capping a stack of teacups on the shrine steps outside Grandma Kane's hall. Two cups vanish under the pressure, same trick as always, and the cats scatter as the stack settles low. She counts what is left before ringing the bell: <kanji>six</kanji> teacups, six things, capped for good.
muttsu.reading_mnemonic: 六 reads むっ here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>むっつ</reading>」.

nan.meaning_mnemonic: Cats keep arriving on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, and you gave up asking what a cat is hours ago. Every question you have left comes with a number stuck to it: how many cats, what floor they have reached, what time they stop. This is the shape the question takes when a counter follows — what, before counters.
nan.reading_mnemonic: A tiny <reading>nun</reading> has claimed the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and runs it like a ticket window. She will not press a button until you say <reading>なん</reading> and then the counter for what you want, and she makes you start again if you mumble the number.
nan.description: This is the same word as the standalone question, wearing the shape it takes when a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows it. You almost never meet it alone; it arrives glued to whatever is being counted.

nana-v.meaning_mnemonic: By the door of Koichi's konbini, the coat hook is really just one bent nail sticking out of the wall. A delivery driver piles dripping rain jackets onto it between beeps of the till, one after another, until the nail bends almost flat under the weight. You count the jackets before it snaps: <kanji>seven</kanji>, all hanging off one crooked hook.
nana-v.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here is the one you already know from the kanji itself: <reading>なな</reading>.

nanatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The hook by the konbini door already sags under a full row of <kanji>seven</kanji> coats, bent halfway into the wall from the weight. A customer tries to squeeze one more sleeve onto it and the whole thing groans, but the hook holds firm — it was built to carry exactly seven things and not one more.
nanatsu.reading_mnemonic: 七 reads なな here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>ななつ</reading>」.

nani.meaning_mnemonic: A frazzled nanny in the echoing hallways of Sei's school is handed things by a toddler all morning: a wet sock, half a stapler, a beetle that is still alive. She has stopped guessing what any of it is. She just holds each object out at arm's length and asks the one flat question that covers all of it — what.
nani.reading_mnemonic: The same <reading>nanny</reading> takes a night shift at Koichi's konbini, and every time the beeping till coughs up an item she does not recognise she holds it over the onigiri shelf and says <reading>なに</reading> at the ceiling. By closing she has said it forty times and solved nothing.
nani.description: On its own — as a bare question, or with most particles — the word takes this reading. When a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows, it switches to the shorter reading you learn separately.

nannji.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the <kanji>time</kanji>-sun still crawls its slow arc overhead. A dazed tourist wanders in, squinting up, unable to read a single hour off it, and grabs a passing cat to blurt the same question over and over: what <kanji>time</kanji> is it? Her whole visit is just that one question: what time.
nannji.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, a jetlagged traveler keeps calling to her grandmother, 'Nan, gee, what time is it?' — sliding into <reading>Nan-gee</reading> each time. The cats now answer back with that same sound, <reading>なんじ</reading>, since that's all anyone there asks: what time.

nanoka.meaning_mnemonic: The bent nail hook holds seven coats until one more lands and it creaks under the weight, confirming <kanji>seven</kanji>. Framed just behind it, the window's bar lets the <kanji>sun</kanji> through for one more <kanji>day</kanji> to close out — seven coats, seven days, the 7th of the month.
nanoka.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the enormous bell tolls seven times, and on the last strike she looks up bewildered and mutters '<reading>Nan, oh, kah</reading>?' — her way of asking if it's really day seven already. The cats don't answer, and <reading>なのか</reading> is what she calls the day from then on.

naze.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in his line for the ninth time and finds nothing but a waterlogged boot, same as the last eight. He doesn't swear, doesn't sigh — he just plants his feet in the mud, glares at the current, and asks the only question left standing: why.
naze.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>なぜ</reading>.
naze.description: なぜ reads as blunter and more formal than a casual why — common in writing, official questions, and pointed interrogation. Dropped into an ordinary chat with a friend, on its own it can land as accusatory rather than merely curious.

neko.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, cats already outnumber worshippers, but one has decided the offering bell is a toy. She swats the rope, ducks under the railing, and curls up exactly where the incense smoke is warmest, ignoring every polite attempt to shoo her off. That smug, entitled little squatter is what cat means.
neko.reading_mnemonic: A visitor watches the shrine cat arch and stretch across the warm stone and winces, worried for her <reading>neck, oh</reading> — just as the cat flops flatter, completely unbothered. That half-panicked warning is the shape of <reading>ねこ</reading>, and the cat never once looks up to acknowledge it.

ni-v.meaning_mnemonic: The waiter arrives to ask how many are dining and finds his answer already snapped in half on the table: two chopsticks, a short one laid over a long one, matching exactly like the pair of raccoons who broke them that way. He doesn't need to count paws underneath — the <kanji>two</kanji> sticks already told him. Table for two.
ni-v.reading_mnemonic: 二 alone already reads <reading>に</reading>, the same reading it carried in the chopstick story — nothing new to learn here.

nichiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: You peer through a window at the <kanji>sun</kanji>, only to realize it is just a painting inside a massive <kanji>weekday</kanji> calendar square. Before you can process the trick, a real <kanji>sun</kanji> rises behind it and sets the whole paper structure on fire to celebrate Sunday.
nichiyoubi.reading_mnemonic: You already know the readings for the kanji in this word, so you just put them together to get <reading>にちようび</reading>.

niku.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer piles his arms so high with packages that he can't see over the top, and the automatic door doesn't slide open fast enough — he plows into the glass, packages skidding toward the onigiri shelf while the till keeps beeping through the whole thing. What he was hoarding, glass door and all, was meat.
niku.reading_mnemonic: The butcher restocking that counter introduces himself as <reading>Nick</reading>, and every time he says it, it comes out clipped and flat, almost like <reading>にく</reading> — the customers just nod along, since that's also the word for the meat piled in front of him.

niwa.meaning_mnemonic: Behind Sei's school, past the sports field, there's a locked gate nobody bothers with anymore. Squeeze through and you find a garden gone completely wild — tomato vines swallowing the old goalposts, cats sunbathing on a rusted rake nobody put away. Teachers pretend it isn't there. Everyone else just calls it the yard behind the yard.
niwa.reading_mnemonic: In that tangled garden behind the school, a cat pounces off the rusted rake and lands wrong, yowling <reading>knee, wah!</reading> — that garbled yelp is exactly the sound of <reading>にわ</reading>, the overgrown little yard where the school's stray cats actually live.

nomimono.meaning_mnemonic: That same yawning mouth wanders down to the riverbank on a hot afternoon, tips its head all the way back over the water, and doesn't stop until the whole river's worth has vanished down its throat. Food sits forgotten beside it; the only thing that gaping mouth wants now is to <kanji>drink</kanji>, and it does, all afternoon, without ever closing once.
nomimono.reading_mnemonic: A stubborn <reading>gnome</reading> in a one-piece <reading>mono</reading> suit haunts the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, feeding it coin after coin. Ask what he's doing up there and he just holds up a can and says <reading>のみもの</reading> — drink — like that explains everything, which, to him, it does.

nooto.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid staples every loose page from their bag into one brick-thick block and hauls it to class insisting it's still light. The teacher weighs it in one hand, sighs, and writes "notebook" across the cover so nobody has to argue about what to call it again.
nooto.reading_mnemonic: Written in kana exactly as it sounds, straight from the English word notebook — read it as <reading>ノート</reading>, no decoding needed.

oba.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an aunt turns up every New Year wrapped in an absurd sheep-print scarf. The temple cats scatter, certain a sheep has invaded their mossy steps. Flustered, she throws up both hands and calls out across the courtyard — that startled, scarf-wrapped arrival is exactly who aunt means.
oba.reading_mnemonic: As the cats bolt, she cries <reading>Oh, baa!</reading> — sheep noise, not sheep, just her own flustered yelp. That startled cry, <reading>おば</reading>, is the exact sound of an aunt arriving at Grandma Kane's shrine every single year, scarf and all.
oba.description: The vowel here is short — don't stretch it into the longer sound used for the word for grandmother. They look and sound almost identical on the page but name different relatives, so lean on the mnemonic's short, startled yelp to keep the vowel length honest.

obaasan.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank where the washing happens, an old woman scrubs scarves for the whole village and refuses anyone's help. Children stop to greet her properly before crossing, and she waves them on with damp hands. To everyone nearby, respectfully, she's simply grandmother — polite, warm, and impossible to argue with.
obaasan.reading_mnemonic: おばあさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おばあさん</reading> read straight through.
obaasan.description: おばあさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly woman, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "ma'am" than a strict family term.

ocha.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she pours something pale green and steaming into small cups for every visitor who climbs the mossy steps, cats sniffing at the tray. One sip after the climb and you understand why she never skips this step: tea.
ocha.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hot can rolls off the shelf and lands right at your feet, steam still hissing from the seam. You yelp <reading>oh, cha!</reading> as it burns your fingers picking it up. That yelp is the reading: <reading>おちゃ</reading>.
ocha.description: Almost always appears with the honorific prefix お attached — daily speech rarely uses the bare form alone, even though it exists in other compounds.

oji.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the point where most people turn back, a man in hiking boots is refilling the lone vending machine himself — turns out it's your uncle, who apparently owns the machine and hikes up every week just to restock it. Nobody in the family questions this anymore. That's just what your uncle does.
oji.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker rounds the last switchback and yelps, oh, gee, at the stranger already there. It's not a stranger — it's your uncle, and that startled gasp is exactly <reading>おじ</reading>: <reading>oh, gee</reading>, uncle, fancy meeting you up here.
oji.description: 叔父 marks a younger uncle — your parent's younger brother, or one married in — as distinct from the term for an older uncle, though both get shortened to the same casual address form in speech.

ojiisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the old bell-ringer finally hands the rope to someone new: a stooped man with a walking stick who has swept the mossy steps every morning for forty years. The cats accept him instantly. The children bow and call him grandfather, and from that day the enormous bell is his alone to ring.
ojiisan.reading_mnemonic: おじいさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おじいさん</reading> read straight through.
ojiisan.description: おじいさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly man, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "grandpa" than a strict family term.

okaasan.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a boy collapses by the lone vending machine, certain he can't take one more step. Then his mother crests the rise behind him, unbothered, carrying his backpack, her water bottle, and a spare pair of socks, somehow not out of breath. That endless, unglamorous readiness is what mother (polite) means.
okaasan.reading_mnemonic: Driving the mountain trail's last hairpin toward the vending machine at the top, she doesn't slow down. The kids in the back seat brace and yell <reading>oh, car, san</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>おかあさん</reading> sounds, screamed by children who have done this drive with her before.

okashi.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone leaves rice crackers by the bell as an offering. A <kanji>child</kanji> wriggles free of its wrap — arms flung wide, the exact shape that means <kanji>child</kanji> — snatches the whole plate and is found later face-down in crumbs. The monks give up on real food; now they just leave out sweets.
okashi.reading_mnemonic: Behind Koichi's konbini, there's a locked drawer everyone whispers about. Pry it open and you find <reading>おかし</reading> — an entire <reading>cache</reading> of sweets he's been hoarding since spring, more candy than any kid could eat in a year.

okusan.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, a woman leans against the lone vending machine, patient in the shade of an oak, clearly waiting for somebody. Every exhausted hiker who finally staggers up assumes she must belong to whoever shows up gasping right after — and that assumption, someone waiting up there for her other half, is exactly (someone's) wife.
okusan.reading_mnemonic: She waves at the oak baking in the noon sun and calls down the trail, <reading>oak sun</reading> — the greeting that carries all the way to the switchbacks. That call is just how <reading>おくさん</reading> sounds: someone's wife, waiting patiently at the top for him to catch up.
okusan.description: 奥さん is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's wife — never your own. It also gets used casually to address a married woman in general, but it is not what a man calls his own wife.

onaka.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a man buys every onigiri on the shelf and eats them standing at the counter, one after another, until his shirt stops closing. By the last one his middle has ballooned into a round drum he has to hold with both hands — his stomach, full past reason, the only thing left worth talking about.
onaka.reading_mnemonic: Koichi watches the man's belly swell round as a spare tire and mutters he looks like he's got one strapped <reading>on a car</reading>. The man just groans <reading>おなか</reading>, patting the bulge, and Koichi decides that's as good a name for it as any.

oneesan.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the captain of the school relay team, the one every younger kid looks up to and never dares call by her first name. She lines up the little ones, ties their shoelaces, and lets them win. That respectful, polite way you address someone's honored older sister is exactly this word.
oneesan.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, the team captain warms up by impersonating a horse, letting out an exaggerated <reading>neigh</reading> before every sprint. The younger kids salute her respectfully as <reading>おねえさん</reading>, the neighing captain, and nobody questions it.
oneesan.description: This word is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's older sister, or an unrelated older woman as a term of respect — it is not the plain, private term you'd use among your own family growing up with a younger sibling.

oniisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a young man rings the enormous bell for an elderly stranger who can't reach the rope, then carries her offering up the mossy steps himself while the shrine cats trail behind them. Nobody there is related to him, but everyone calls him older brother (polite) anyway, because that is simply what the word is for.
oniisan.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats climb his leg the moment he sits on the mossy steps, and he winces <reading>oh, knee, sahn</reading> as claws land — which is exactly how <reading>おにいさん</reading> sounds, and exactly why the cats never leave him alone.
oniisan.description: The polite, respectful form used to talk about or address someone else's older brother, or a young man in general as a courteous form of address — contrast with the plain word used only for your own older brother.

onnanohito.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> finally rises from her bow and falls into step beside the two legs she already knows as a <kanji>person</kanji>, the pair of them striding together past the cats toward the enormous bell. Kneeling figure plus striding legs, moving as one down the mossy steps — that's a grown woman.
onnanohito.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのひと</reading>.

onnanoko.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a tiny figure copies the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> pose out on the sports field, except her sweeping arm has curled inward to cradle a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, little arms flung out against her chest. A pint-sized woman who still has a bundled baby's shape tucked in her arms — that's a girl.
onnanoko.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのこ</reading>.

osake.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats curled by the enormous bell always find the one jar the priest forgot to lock away. By the time you arrive for New Year's prayers, three of them are sprawled belly-up on the mossy steps, hiccuping softly, radiating that unmistakable warm reek of alcohol.
osake.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane spots the empty jar and gasps <reading>Oh, sake</reading>, her shocked cry stretching into <reading>おさけ</reading> as she chases the wobbling cats down the mossy steps, the enormous bell clanging behind her the whole way.
osake.description: お酒 means alcohol in general — beer, wine, spirits, anything you drink to get tipsy — not only the rice wine English speakers picture when they hear the word sake.

otearai.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a door stands with a huge <kanji>hand</kanji> painted on it, fingers spread wide and dripping wet. Everyone in line shakes that dripping <kanji>hand</kanji> before ducking inside to hunt for the toilet. The dripping hand is the whole point of the sign: wash first, then go — this is the restroom.
otearai.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a visitor doubles over on the mossy steps and yells <reading>oh, tea-uh-rye!</reading> — the cats scatter as she sprints past the enormous bell, shouting the word for restroom: <reading>おてあらい</reading>, praying she makes it past every last cat in time.

otokonohito.meaning_mnemonic: Out in the paddy, the <kanji>man</kanji> finally straightens up from the plow, gives his arm one last flex, and starts walking toward Koichi's konbini for something cold — those two legs carrying him off the field are exactly the <kanji>person</kanji> he becomes the second he stops working. Power in the field, then legs on the road: that's a grown man.
otokonohito.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのひと</reading>.

otokonoko.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, a small figure flexes one arm at the vending machine exactly like the <kanji>man</kanji> dragging his plow through the paddy, except his other arm is still tucked into a <kanji>child</kanji>'s swaddle, wriggling loose at his side. A miniature man who hasn't finished unwrapping yet — that's a boy.
otokonoko.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのこ</reading>.

otona.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward suddenly stops and throws their arms out wide, legs spread as far as they'll go — the stance for showing off something <kanji>big</kanji>. Nobody teaches a kid to stand like that; you grow into needing the room. Standing tall enough to need the whole stance is what makes you an adult.
otona.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby stops wailing the second someone hands him <reading>a tuna</reading> — the calm is instant, like a switch. Jin ducks through the doorway just in time to see it: <reading>おとな</reading>, grown up right in front of him.

ototoi.meaning_mnemonic: The smug goat is certain her one-contestant talent show already happened — she just can't recall which sun-window <kanji>day</kanji> it played in. She backs through yesterday's window, then one more window behind that, since in her world there is only ever <kanji>one</kanji> winner. Two windows back is where she finds it: the day before yesterday.
ototoi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a scruffy otter drags the same battered toy from the water, swearing it's the first time. The other otters know better — they watched that toy sink two mornings back, on <reading>おととい</reading>, and nobody tells the <reading>otter</reading> <reading>toy</reading> story twice.

otousan.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, red-faced and sweating under the noon sun, a father hauls a stalled cart the last hundred meters by rope while his kid cheers from beside the lone vending machine. That's the picture pinned to father, polite: the dad you'd point out respectfully to a stranger, not the tired grumble you'd use at home.
otousan.reading_mnemonic: As he heaves the cart past the vending machine, the kid shouts the word for him, and it lands in your ear as <reading>oh, tow, sun</reading> — dad towing, sun blazing overhead — the same beats as <reading>おとうさん</reading>. That's the polite word for pointing him out to a stranger on the trail, not the plain one for talking about your own.
otousan.description: お父さん (otousan) is the polite, respectful word for father — what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father in conversation. It contrasts with the plain 父 (chichi), which you use only when talking about your own father to people outside the family.

otouto.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the pesky little brother who trails you everywhere, small enough that shopkeepers assume he's still in diapers, always demanding you carry him piggyback until your arms give out. That exact whiny, tag-along presence is what points straight at a younger brother.
otouto.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the small brother stomps on the same customer's foot twice reaching for onigiri, and the customer yelps <reading>oh, toe, toe</reading> each time. The beeping till clerk sighs and says it again, plain: <reading>おとうと</reading>, always causing trouble.

otto.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman is washing laundry when her husband wades in fully dressed, chasing a sock that floated loose, soaking his only good shirt in the process. She doesn't even look up — of course that's who waded in after one sock, nobody else would bother. That reliable, faintly ridiculous devotion is (my) husband.
otto.reading_mnemonic: He climbs out of the river dripping head to toe, sock triumphantly in hand, and she just sighs, <reading>Otto</reading>, not again — the exact sound of <reading>おっと</reading>, her name for the husband who always wades in after the laundry.
otto.description: 夫 is the plain way a wife refers to her own husband when speaking to other people — not a word she'd use to call out to him directly, and not used for someone else's husband.

pan.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer grabs the last loaf off the shelf right as the till starts beeping, panicking because the shelf is otherwise all onigiri. He hugs it like it's the only bread left in Japan, mutters thanks under the fluorescent lights, and pays before anyone else spots it.
pan.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read: <reading>パン</reading>, borrowed straight from Portuguese pão — no derivation needed.

pasokon.meaning_mnemonic: In Koichi's konbini, beside the onigiri shelf, a customer heaves a slab of grey plastic onto the counter and starts jabbing it the way he jabs the beeping till. Half-finished English stutters out of its little speaker — pa, so, kon — until the whole register short-circuits into a glowing screen full of spreadsheets: a computer, ringing up groceries nobody asked it to buy.
pasokon.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, no kanji hiding underneath — just the borrowed English squeezed down to fit: <reading>パソコン</reading>.

pen.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine sells exactly one item no hiker asked for: a pen that leaks the instant you click it, blooming blue across your knuckles and smearing your name across the summit logbook the second you try to sign it — a pen, and now a permanent one.
pen.reading_mnemonic: ペン is kana all the way through, read exactly as written and borrowed straight from English: 「<reading>ペン</reading>」 is simply pen.

raigetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads still waves in every traveler for shade, but tonight it's packed solid. It points up at the crescent overhead and tells the next pair to <kanji>come</kanji> back once that sliver of <kanji>month</kanji> has swung all the way around and grown thin again. That's next month's shade, not this one's.
raigetsu.reading_mnemonic: 来 already gives you らい and 月 already gives you げつ — stack them straight through into <reading>らいげつ</reading>.

rainen.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads waves its branches at the scarecrow, telling it to <kanji>come</kanji> rest in the shade. The scarecrow yells back that it has to stand in the field for the rest of the <kanji>year</kanji>, but promises to finally take a break next year.
rainen.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly what you learned for the kanji: 来 (らい) plus 年 (ねん) makes <reading>らいねん</reading>.

raishuu.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads is still waving <kanji>come</kanji> at anyone nearby, but now it's leaning off the far edge of the calendar page, calling toward the square just past the current loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> — beckoning travelers to a loop that hasn't even started. Next week.
raishuu.reading_mnemonic: 来 already carries the らい reading and 週 already carries the しゅう reading, so stacked together in order they simply give you <reading>らいしゅう</reading> — no story needed.

rajio.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the one enormous bell hasn't been rung in months, yet the cats gather on the mossy steps every evening at six, ears flat, tails puffed. Tucked behind the bell sits a cracked wooden box quietly muttering a weather report to no one. The cats, it turns out, have been listening to the shrine's radio the whole time.
rajio.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ラジオ</reading> is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so the reading is simply <reading>ラジオ</reading> itself — nothing to derive.

rei.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a ranger posts an official notice board each morning with the exact temperature. One frost-bitten dawn, the mercury refuses to rise past the middle line at all, and the ranger stamps the report with one stiff, formal number before trudging back down. That number is zero.
rei.reading_mnemonic: The ranger reading the thermometer is named Ray, and he announces temperatures stiffly, formally, no contractions ever. He reads the number in one clipped word, <reading>れい</reading> — <reading>Ray</reading> only sounds this formal when the mercury freezes at zero.
rei.description: 零 is the formal, written register for zero — the word you'd see on an official temperature report or hear in a stiff announcement, not the one you'd use casually reading out a phone number or a game score.

resutoran.meaning_mnemonic: Someone moors a floating diner to a post on the riverbank so it can't drift off. A chalkboard menu hangs from the mast, and the one waiter wades out in rubber boots to deliver plates. Tourists queue on the bank just to eat somewhere that technically counts as a restaurant, even though it's really a raft with silverware.
resutoran.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>レストラン</reading>.
resutoran.description: レストラン specifically means a Western-style sit-down restaurant. Casual Japanese eateries, noodle counters, and specialty food shops usually go by other names, not this word.

roku-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, eight cats are sprawled across the mossy steps at dawn. She sets the heavy iron offering lid down with a clang right on the top step, and two cats bolt at the sound, tails high. What's left staring up at the enormous bell is <kanji>six</kanji> cats, thoroughly unimpressed by the racket. The lid on top of eight, as always, leaves <kanji>six</kanji>.
roku-v.reading_mnemonic: 六's reading here is just the number's own reading you already learned: <reading>ろく</reading>.

ryouri.meaning_mnemonic: It's 2 a.m. at Koichi's konbini, fluorescent lights buzzing over the onigiri shelf while the till beeps through a lull. Bored, the night clerk pulls ingredients off the shelves — instant miso, a rice ball, a squeeze of mayo — and assembles them into something new on the counter. By closing, he's turned convenience-store scraps into an actual dish: cooking.
ryouri.reading_mnemonic: The clerk introduces himself over the counter, 'I'm <reading>Leo Uri</reading>, konbini cooking champion of aisle three.' He says his name so fast it comes out as one word — <reading>りょうり</reading> — which is exactly how you ask for cooking or a dish.

saifu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone wading across loses their footing, and a slim leather fold flies from their pocket mid-splash. Coins scatter into the current and bills drift downstream like paper boats, but the fold itself washes up on the bank, empty and dripping — proof that whatever it once held, it's still a wallet.
saifu.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, an old peddler unzips a battered leather fold and swears it's <reading>sci-fi</reading> tech from the future. He says the word for it, <reading>さいふ</reading>, slow and dramatic, then just buys a can of coffee like it's an ordinary wallet after all.

sakana.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman casts his line for hours and reels in nothing but weeds, until a sudden tug nearly drags him into the water — he hauls back to find something flopping on the bank, gasping right alongside him. That flopping, gasping catch is the entire reason anyone stands at a riverbank all afternoon: fish.
sakana.reading_mnemonic: The fisherwoman working that same riverbank, <reading>Sock Anna</reading>, wades in after a lost sock and something latches onto her bare foot instead of the fabric — she yelps out the same sound as her own name, <reading>さかな</reading>, and from then on that's just the word for fish.

san-v.meaning_mnemonic: A teacher taps a chalk pointer against three stacked lines on the board, one, two, three, and by the third tap the class already knows what word is coming before she says it. There is no trick to uncover here: <kanji>three</kanji> lines stacked in a character just spells the word three, plainly, the way it has all along.
san-v.reading_mnemonic: 三 alone already reads <reading>さん</reading>, the same reading you counted out tapping the three lines.

satou.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone drops a paper packet off the little footbridge, and instead of sinking it dissolves mid-air into the current, turning a whole stretch of water thick and slow, the fish drifting through it like it's honey — that's what falls into your tea as sugar.
satou.reading_mnemonic: Sei's homeroom teacher introduces herself as <reading>Sato</reading>-sensei, then skips the chalkboard and just pours a spoonful into her tea to prove the name: <reading>さとう</reading>, she says, tapping the packet, sweet like she is.

seito.meaning_mnemonic: That same patch of earth where a seed splits open into <kanji>life</kanji> now stretches out as a schoolyard, planted with row after row of identical green shoots, all still too short to see over the fence. They're not finished yet — still rooted, still waiting their turn to grow — and that half-grown state is exactly what a pupil is.
seito.reading_mnemonic: At the school, a mob of first-years shuffles so close behind <reading>Sei</reading> that they keep landing on her <reading>toe</reading> — "say... toe!" she yelps each time. The name sticks: these tagalong underclassmen following the star student's every step become known as 「<reading>せいと</reading>」.

sen-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine's price display multiplies without warning: one bold slash scratches straight across the readout, the same slash that once capped that plus-sign cross into something bigger, and the number keeps climbing past every digit until it locks on one round <kanji>thousand</kanji> and finally stops beeping.
sen-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 千 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>せん</reading>.

sengetsu.meaning_mnemonic: Those two legs, already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone, are long gone before you've even reached the door. By the time you catch up, the sliver of <kanji>month</kanji> they left under has faded to nothing and grown back new. Whatever they did, they did it under last month's crescent.
sengetsu.reading_mnemonic: 先 already gives you せん and 月 already gives you げつ — lay them end to end into <reading>せんげつ</reading>.

sensei.meaning_mnemonic: The legs that always stride out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone reach the classroom first, plant themselves at the front, and refuse to sit down. Beneath their feet is the same patch of ground where a seed cracks open into <kanji>life</kanji> — because this is the one person whose ideas take root in you and grow. That's a teacher.
sensei.reading_mnemonic: 先 gives せん and 生 supplies the same せい you know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student — stack them together and you get exactly 「<reading>せんせい</reading>」.

senshuu.meaning_mnemonic: Those <kanji>previous</kanji> legs are at it again, always a step ahead — they've already marched clear across the loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> on the calendar page and finished tracing it before you woke up. By the time you look at the grid, that loop is closed and cold. Last week.
senshuu.reading_mnemonic: 先 already carries the せん reading and 週 already carries the しゅう reading, so stacked together in order they simply give you <reading>せんしゅう</reading> — no story needed.

shashin.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a dozen cats sprawl across the mossy steps, and just as the great bell tolls, a bulb pops and freezes every yawn and twitching tail at once, the whole moment trapped flat and still forever. That frozen instant, kept for good, is a photograph.
shashin.reading_mnemonic: A tourist barges into the shrine's hush, camera raised, and the old priest just hisses <reading>shush in</reading> before you break it — too late, the shutter already clicked. He hands back the camera; the saved file reads simply <reading>しゃしん</reading>.

shatsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer leans too far over the counter to grab an onigiri and his loose top catches on the price scanner by the till. The register beeps furiously, over and over, as if trying to ring up the fabric itself, until Koichi peels the sleeve free and holds up the wrinkled shirt like it just came off the shelf.
shatsu.reading_mnemonic: シャツ is written the way it sounds — no kanji to decode, just read the kana straight across as <reading>シャツ</reading>.

shi-num.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the same sealed box waits among the mossy steps, its trapped mouth still murmuring numbers into the corner. A cat swats it off the step and the lid cracks — the mouth peeks out just far enough to hiss a hushed <kanji>four</kanji> before a monk claps the lid shut, refusing to let it say the number again.
shi-num.reading_mnemonic: That hushed <reading>し</reading> is the same reading 四 already taught you — the clipped <reading>shh</reading> the monk uses to cut the mouth off mid-count.
shi-num.description: This reading of 四 sounds identical to a much darker word, so hospitals, hotels, and gift-givers avoid it — floor numbers, room numbers, and counted items switch to the other reading, よん, instead. Learn to recognize both, but default to よん when you're the one speaking.

shichi-num.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, the same bent-nail hook holds gym jerseys instead of coats. There's only one hook by the lockers, so seven players fresh off the field cram their jerseys onto it at once, the nail sagging nearly sideways under the pile. The coach counts before it gives way: <kanji>seven</kanji> jerseys, all balanced on one crooked hook.
shichi-num.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here keeps the reading you already learned for formal counting: <reading>しち</reading>.
shichi-num.description: しち is the older, more formal reading of 七 — used in compounds, in reading dates and times aloud, and in fixed set phrases. なな is generally preferred when counting items alone or aloud, since しち can be mistaken for the word for one in quick speech.

shinbun.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone <kanji>new</kanji> in town stands beaming beside a fresh stack of printed pages, and every cat under the big bell presses an ear to the stack like it's a gate, straining to <kanji>hear</kanji> what's inside before anyone thinks to ask. By the time the bell rings, the whole shrine already knows what's inside those pages pressed flat — the newspaper.
shinbun.reading_mnemonic: 新聞 keeps both taught readings back to back, so read it as <reading>しんぶん</reading> — new, then hear.

shio.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn at Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cats watch her fling a scoop of coarse white grains across the gate, a purifying toss meant to sting bare skin. One greedy cat licks a stray grain from the stone, recoils hard, and spends the hour draining the well dry. That sharp mineral bite on its tongue is salt.
shio.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane hands her shrine attendant Ren a sack for the purification toss. He trips on the steps, and it bursts everywhere as he yelps '<reading>She, oh!</reading>' watching grains fill his sandals — that yelp is exactly <reading>しお</reading>, salt.

shokuji.meaning_mnemonic: At exactly noon a bell rings through Sei's school, and dozens of <kanji>eat</kanji> tents pop up along the hallway floor — the same roof-made-of-dinner shelter you already know, one for every student ducking in to eat. Trays pile up under each roof until the bell rings again. That whole stretch, from first bite to last, is the meal.
shokuji.reading_mnemonic: A student named Shoko checks her watch in the echoing hallway and gasps '<reading>Shock, gee</reading>, is it that late already?' — she's smelling the trays before she sees them. That gasp is exactly <reading>しょくじ</reading>: meal.

shuumatsu.meaning_mnemonic: You trace the winding path for the <kanji>week</kanji> until you run out of calendar page completely and your finger slips off the paper. Dropping off the edge of that grid lands you right in the weekend.
shuumatsu.reading_mnemonic: You spend your entire weekend at the riverbank scrubbing the mud out of your car's <reading>shoe mats</reading> (<reading>しゅうまつ</reading>). You wash them for two days straight, completely ruining your actual weekend.

sobo.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till goes quiet as an elderly woman counts her coins one by one. Koichi leans over to the new hire and says simply: that's my grandmother, in for her onigiri. No polite title, no fuss — just family, plain and direct, the way you describe your own grandmother to someone else.
sobo.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old woman mutters sew, bow, sew, bow while stitching ribbons onto scarves. A child mishears the rhythm as <reading>そぼ</reading>, the word for grandmother, and now everyone at the water's edge calls her the <reading>sew-bow</reading> lady who happens to be somebody's grandmother too.
sobo.description: 祖母 is how you refer to your own grandmother when speaking to someone outside the family — plain and humble, with no polite title attached. It isn't what you'd call her directly, or use for someone else's grandmother, both of which take an address term instead.

sochira.meaning_mnemonic: You're already at Koichi's till, practically leaning on the register, when you ask where the onigiri is. Koichi doesn't even look up — he just tilts his chin two feet toward the shelf you're basically touching and grunts the sound out, because when the thing you want is that close, all you need to say is that way.
sochira.reading_mnemonic: You already know そ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>そちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"so-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no twist to catch you out.

sofu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the old man who rings Grandma Kane's one enormous shrine bell every single morning, out of habit rather than faith, then complains for an hour that his arm hurts. That specific, grumbling, ritual-bound old man is exactly your grandfather.
sofu.reading_mnemonic: After ringing the enormous bell, the old man collapses onto the shrine steps and announces he's <reading>so full</reading> — of aches, not food. The cats ignore him as he mutters it again, <reading>そふ</reading>, and refuses to get up.

soko.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone drops a sandal mid-crossing and it snags on a rock partway across the water. You point at the exact spot from the near bank, arm out straight, calling out to the person wading in: there, there, no, THERE — the sandal never moves, but your pointing finger fixes the place for good.
soko.reading_mnemonic: そこ is written entirely in kana the way it sounds, with no kanji standing behind it — you read <reading>そこ</reading> exactly as it's spelled.

sonna.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat knocks the enormous bell clean off its stand, and when she's told it was an accident she just stares at the wreckage — that kind of excuse, the kind aimed right back at whoever just spoke, never quite convincing her.
sonna.reading_mnemonic: Like its cousins, this word is pure kana, so <reading>そんな</reading> is pronounced exactly as spelled, with nothing underneath to decode.

sono.meaning_mnemonic: Your friend is squatting on the riverbank with three soaked shoes lined up beside them, and you are holding a sonar gun that refuses to lock onto anything near you. It only pings at objects sitting next to somebody else, whining so-no, so-no as it swings toward them. Whatever it picks out is that shoe, that bucket, that dripping thing over by your friend.
sono.reading_mnemonic: No decoding needed: this word is spelled in kana precisely as it is pronounced, <reading>その</reading>.
sono.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something in the listener's zone rather than yours, so a thing in their hand or on their side of the table takes this word even where English would say this. It also picks up something the other person has just mentioned, with nothing visible to point at.

sora.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail sits improbably alone, no building for a mile around it, just a cable running to nowhere and a stretch of blue that starts at the machine's roof and doesn't stop. Hikers reach the summit less for the drinks than to stand there and stare straight up into all that open sky.
sora.reading_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, a hawk seen every clear afternoon <reading>soars</reading> straight up until it's a speck, and the hikers waiting on their drink call it their <reading>そら</reading> bird, because it never comes down until the whole open expanse above the machine is empty again.

sore.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer holds an onigiri up under your nose, and your pointing finger is so sore from a full shift at the beeping till that you can barely straighten it. You waggle the sore finger at the rice ball sitting there in his hands and grunt. Whatever is over by him, close enough for him to touch — that one.
sore.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>それ</reading>, so there is no reading to decode.
sore.description: Points at something near the person you are talking to, rather than near you — the middle rung of the near, middle, far set. It stands alone as a pronoun, so it never sits directly in front of a noun; the form that does that is a separate word.

suiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>weekday</kanji>, you stand by the riverbank to watch the <kanji>sun</kanji> come up, but today a massive geyser of freezing <kanji>water</kanji> blasts out of the river and knocks you flat into the mud. You scrape yourself off, remembering that this mid-week flood always happens on Wednesday.
suiyoubi.reading_mnemonic: There are no new sounds to learn here, just combine the kanji readings you already know into <reading>すいようび</reading>.

suupaa.meaning_mnemonic: A shopping cart rolls out the automatic doors hauling forty bags of rice, an entire side of beef, and a wobbling pyramid of soap boxes, because an ordinary grocery run won't cut it here. One roof, every aisle, everything in bulk — the store is proud enough of the scale to call itself super for it: a supermarket.
suupaa.reading_mnemonic: スーパー is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>super</reading> and you've already said <reading>スーパー</reading>, nothing to derive.

tabemono.meaning_mnemonic: That tent pitched over a heaped tray — the shelter you duck into when you're hungry — gets dragged whole onto Sei's school sports field for a picnic, roof and all. The whole team ducks under it at once, and every dish sitting under that roof, from the rice down to the last pickle, gets <kanji>eaten</kanji> before the bell rings. Anything that ends up under that tent is, simply, food.
tabemono.reading_mnemonic: Every lunch break, a scrawny transfer student named <reading>Toby Moreno</reading> materializes at Koichi's konbini and buys out the entire onigiri shelf without saying a word. The clerk has started calling out <reading>たべもの</reading> the second the bell rings, because that name and that hunger always arrive together.

takushii.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail is so steep that hikers stop believing in the vending machine at the top — until a taxi comes crawling up the switchbacks behind them, meter running, wheels spinning on loose gravel. It pulls up right next to the machine and idles patiently, because someone actually ordered a taxi to fetch canned coffee from the summit.
takushii.reading_mnemonic: This word is a loanword borrowed straight from English "taxi" and written in katakana exactly as it's read: <reading>タクシー</reading>.

tamago.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the delivery truck arrives before dawn and unloads crate after crate of impossibly round, pale ovals, still warm from the truck's engine. Koichi holds one to the fluorescent light, taps it once, and it cracks open — bright yolk sliding across the counter: egg.
tamago.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the fat shrine cat curls into the offering bowl every morning. Someone finally claps and shouts <reading>Tama, go!</reading> — it slinks off, revealing one warm egg underneath. That shout is the reading: <reading>たまご</reading>.

te-v.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> is still hanging out mid-air, wrist and all, waiting for the shake nobody's ever finished. It doesn't close, it doesn't wave — it just stays there, open-palmed, being exactly the shape it always was. That patient, unshaken shape is the word for hand.
te-v.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same lesson: 手 already gave you two readings, and this word just borrows the plain <reading>て</reading> reading straight off it.

teeburu.meaning_mnemonic: Two fishermen haul a wide, flat plank out of the river and can't be bothered carrying it back to camp, so they wedge it level across four boulders right there on the bank and eat lunch off it. Every trip after, they head straight for the same plank on the same four rocks. They never call it a plank again, it's their table.
teeburu.reading_mnemonic: This word is a straight loanword from the English word for table, written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>テーブル</reading>.

tegami.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a <kanji>hand</kanji> reaches across the water and drops a folded page into a second <kanji>hand</kanji> waiting on the far bank, which folds it again and passes it to a third — the page crossing hand to hand until it reaches you, refolded and ready to read: a letter.
tegami.reading_mnemonic: Koichi wraps a sticky gummy candy inside a folded note at the konbini register and mutters <reading>the gummy</reading> as he slides it across the counter — the customer unwraps it, and taped underneath, waiting to be read, is a <reading>てがみ</reading>.

tenki.meaning_mnemonic: Look up past the ceiling stretched over everyone's outstretched arms — the <kanji>sky</kanji> itself — and you'll see it has moods. When that same curling wisp of <kanji>spirit</kanji> that rises off a hot bowl of rice thickens into cloud, or thins and vanishes, the sky is telling you what's coming: today's weather.
tenki.reading_mnemonic: 天 already gives you てん and 気 already lends Kiki's き — stitch them together and you get <reading>てんき</reading>, weather.

terebi.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail breaks down one rainy week, and its cracked screen fills with fuzzy grey static instead of dispensing canned coffee. Hikers keep climbing anyway, huddling round the glowing box, because somehow it has started showing Sei's sports day live from the valley below. Nobody's brave enough to unplug the trail's new TV.
terebi.reading_mnemonic: <reading>テレビ</reading> is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so the reading is simply <reading>テレビ</reading> itself — nothing to derive.

toire.meaning_mnemonic: The bell rings at Sei's school and the hallway turns into a stampede — everyone sprinting for the same door before the next class starts.
